false_positives.candidate:
Attendee email uses subtitle 'emailed you and any other attendees' that is inaccurate for newly added guests

The subtitle text is reused from scheduled emails and the attendee is told they are receiving a calendar invite as in a new booking, but the email payload also sets status CONFIRMED and method REQUEST, which is a fresh invite for an existing event; behavior is questionable for existing attendees.

Calendar attendees updated before the guests are validated/persisted correctly and with no error handling

updateCalendarAttendees is awaited without try/catch, so any calendar provider failure makes the mutation throw after the attendees were already written to the DB, leaving the client seeing an error while guests were actually added. Also the handler uses the original booking object (before the new attendees) for eventManager, so calendar sync may not include the new guests.

Crash when attendees array is empty

this.calEvent.attendees[0].name dereferences index 0 without a guard; a booking with no attendees would throw inside getNodeMailerPayload.

Email failure silently swallowed with console.log, losing error details

The catch block logs a fixed string without the error object, so email failures are invisible in logs. Should use the logger and include err.

Error toast message formatting is wrong

The message is built as `${err.data?.code}: ${t(err.message)}`, which is always truthy, so the fallback t("unable_to_add_guests") is never used, and the raw error code prefix is shown to users.

Mutation has no check that bookingId belongs to the caller beyond the handler; guests may be added to any booking

addGuests uses authedProcedure and the handler checks only membership; the attendee check uses user.email on an existing booking and the team check is broken (see AND bug), so the authorization relies on the flawed logic above.

Organizer email subject uses first attendee name, not the new guests

The subject in organizer-add-guests-email.ts uses this.calEvent.attendees[0].name, which is the original booker, while the email is about newly added guests; also the attendees array may be empty causing a runtime crash on [0].name.

Zod schema recreated on every render

ZAddGuestsInputSchema is defined inside the component body and rebuilt each render; it should be hoisted to module scope.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Non-atomic read-modify-write of retryCount

retryCount is incremented using the value read at the start of the run (`reminder.retryCount + 1`) rather than an atomic `{ increment: 1 }` update. If two cron invocations overlap, both can read the same value and write the same increment, undercounting failures and allowing more attempts than the threshold of two.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup deletes any reminder with retryCount > 1, regardless of method or state

The second arm of the deleteMany OR (`retryCount: { gt: 1 }`) has no `method: SMS` filter and no `scheduled`/`cancelled` filter. It deletes any WorkflowReminder row with retryCount > 1 across all methods (EMAIL, WHATSAPP) and in any state. The intent is to drop SMS reminders that failed twice, so the clause should be scoped to `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS, scheduled: false`.

false_positives.candidate:
No tests for the new retry and deletion behavior

The PR changes retry counting, the failure path, and the deletion criteria, but adds no tests. Nothing verifies that a reminder is deleted after two failures, that successful scheduling does not increment the counter, or that non-SMS reminders are untouched.

Reminders with empty message or no sendTo never increment retryCount

The retry increment only happens inside `if (message?.length && sendTo)`. If the message is empty (for example no reminderBody and template is not REMINDER) or sendTo is missing, neither the success nor the failure branch runs and retryCount stays at 0. Such a reminder is picked up on every cron run forever and is never deleted, which is the unbounded-retry problem this PR is meant to fix.

Unguarded retry update in catch can abort the whole cron run

The retryCount update inside the catch block is not wrapped in its own try/catch. If that database write fails (connection issue, deleted row, constraint error), the exception escapes the for-loop, so every remaining unscheduled reminder in the batch is skipped for this run and the handler returns a 500 instead of the 'SMS scheduled' response. One failing reminder can thus block all the others.

`dayjs(date.start).add(...) === dayjs(date.end).add(...)` compares two freshly created Dayjs objects with `===`, which is always false. false_positives.candidate:
No test covers the round-robin fixed-host date override fix

The PR's main claim is that date overrides of fixed hosts now restrict round-robin slots, but the only test added covers the invitee timezone change for a personal event. No test creates a round-robin event with a fixed host having a date override and checks that slots outside the override are removed. The new checkIfIsAvailable override and working-hours logic is therefore untested for the reported bug.

Override day comparison mixes server-local and UTC formatting

The override start is shifted by a computed offset and formatted with `format("YYYY MM DD")` using dayjs's local zone (`dayjs(date.start)` is not `.utc()`), and this is compared against `slotStartTime.format(...)`, which is UTC. The result depends on the server's TZ environment, so on a non-UTC server a date override can match the wrong day or miss the slot entirely. The comparison should be done in a single explicit timezone on both sides.

Override timezone may be undefined and `Date.toString()` round-trip is lossy

`override.timeZone` is optional in `TimeRange`, and `tz(undefined)` silently falls back to the local timezone, which yields a wrong offset. Additionally `override.start.toString()` drops milliseconds and relies on Date string parsing. Use `dayjs(override.start)` directly and handle a missing timezone explicitly (for example, fall back to the organizer timezone).

Shifted override minutes ignore day rollover

The startTime/endTime are computed as `hour()*60 + minute()` after shifting by the timezone offset, which discards the date. If the shifted time crosses midnight (for example, an override at 23:00 organizer time shifted to the next day for the invitee), the minute-of-day wraps to the wrong value, and the override window is placed at the wrong time of day. The override end is similarly affected. Offsets should be applied to the day-based timestamp, not the wrapped clock time.

checkIfIsAvailable now rejects slots outside `workingHours` for every caller, including fixed hosts whose `workingHours` were previously ignored at this point. `slotStartTime.day()` uses UTC weekday and UTC minutes, while `workingHour.startTime/endTime` are minutes in the organizer timezone. For organizers far from UTC, valid slots near midnight will be wrongly rejected or accepted. This is a behavior change beyond the described fix and is not covered by tests.

false_positives.candidate:
A single missing offset permanently stalls commits for the partition

In `get_committable_offsets`, the loop breaks at the first offset that is not in `all_offsets`. Kafka offsets are not guaranteed contiguous (log compaction, transaction control markers, aborted transactions). If an offset is never delivered to `submit`, `highest_committable` never advances past it, and every later offset is treated as blocked forever. Consumer lag then grows without bound and the committed position never moves, so on restart everything after the gap is reprocessed. The tracker should treat the gap as a non-outstanding position, e.g. by advancing over offsets that were never registered and were below the next delivered offset.

Offsets are committed from a background thread, not the processing thread

`_commit_loop` runs in its own thread and calls `self.commit_function(committable)`, which is the arroyo `commit` callable bound to the consumer. Arroyo/Kafka consumer commits are not designed to be called concurrently with the consumer's poll loop from another thread, and the strategy's `poll()`/`submit()` run on the processing thread. This can race with the consumer's own commit/poll or with rebalance handling and produce undefined commit behaviour. Commits should be triggered from the strategy's poll/submit path on the processing thread.

Queues are unbounded, so the advertised backpressure does not exist

The class docstring claims 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but every queue is created with `queue.Queue()` (no maxsize), and `submit` never blocks. The consumer will keep polling and buffering Kafka messages in memory whenever a slow worker falls behind, which can exhaust memory under a backlog. Either bound the queues and block or pause the consumer, or remove the claim from the docstring.

Rebalance/recreate scenario is not tested, which hides the shared-pool shutdown bug

All factory tests create one strategy per factory and shut the factory down at the end. There is no test that calls `create_with_partitions` twice, closes the first strategy, and then submits to the second. Such a test would expose that closing one strategy shuts down the shared queue pool and drops messages.

Shared queue pool is shut down when a rebalance closes the old strategy

`create_thread_queue_parallel_worker` hands the same `self.queue_pool` to every strategy it creates, and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()`/`terminate()` (queue_consumer.py ~lines 335-342) call `queue_pool.shutdown()`. On a Kafka rebalance, arroyo calls `create_with_partitions` again and closes the previous strategy. The old strategy's close shuts down the pool that the new strategy is using. Afterwards `FixedQueuePool.submit` calls `queue.put` on shut-down queues, which raises, and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` logs and silently drops the message while marking its offset complete. Result messages are lost after any rebalance. The pool lifetime needs to be owned by the factory, not by each strategy's close().

Shutdown discards queued work items without draining them

`FixedQueuePool.shutdown` sets `worker.shutdown = True` before shutting down the queues. The worker loop checks that flag before each `get`, so items still queued are abandoned rather than processed. Their offsets are never committed, so they will be reprocessed later. This is safe for at-least-once delivery, but it is not what the 'no item is lost' guarantee in the strategy docstring implies, and nothing logs how many items were dropped.

`pytestmark` on a unittest TestCase class is ineffective and the Kafka test may silently skip or leak topics

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache miss is re-checked only by the fast path, so concurrent callers all rebuild the manifest

The read lock is released at line 43 and the write lock is taken at line 48 without re-checking `entryPointAssetsCache`. When the cache is empty or in dev mode, every goroutine that misses the cache at the same moment proceeds to call readWebAssetsFromFile (or the CDN path) and rebuilds the manifest, one after another. The usual fix is to re-read the cache after acquiring the write lock and return early if it is already populated. This only matters at startup or in dev mode, so the impact is limited to redundant file reads and parsing.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

false_positives.candidate:
No regression test for the data race fix

The PR fixes an unsynchronized read of the package-level `entryPointAssetsCache`, but adds no test that exercises GetWebAssets from multiple goroutines. A test run under `go test -race` that calls GetWebAssets concurrently (with the cache populated and in dev mode) would catch a regression of this fix. Without one, the lock discipline could be broken again silently.

Write lock is held across file and network I/O, blocking all readers

The exclusive lock taken at line 48 is held for the whole rebuild, including the HTTP request in readWebAssetsFromCDN and the file read. Every concurrent GetWebAssets call, including ones that would otherwise hit the cached fast path, blocks on RLock until the rebuild finishes. A slow or hung CDN request, bounded only by the context, can stall all page renders. Consider doing the load outside the lock and only publishing the result under the lock.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions always returns false, so the feature flag check is dead logic

enableSqlExpressions computes `enabled := !IsEnabledGlobally(FlagSqlExpressions)`, then returns false on both branches of `if enabled`. The result is that SQL expressions are unconditionally rejected regardless of the flag. The function reads as if it honours the flag but it does not, so anyone who later re-enables the feature will be confused, and the flag check is misleading. If the intent is a hard disable, the function and the flag lookup should be removed and the SQL case should return the error directly. If the intent is to gate on the flag, the negation and the second `return false` are wrong.

true_positives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Stub DB silently replaces the SQL engine and its errors are not tied to the gate

DB, TablesList, RunCommands and QueryFramesInto are now stubs returning 'not implemented'. TablesList in parser.go and SQLCommand.Execute depend on these. The gate lives only in reader.go's ReadQuery. Other entry points such as UnmarshalSQLCommand and NewSQLCommand reach sql.TablesList without the gate, so they fail with an opaque 'error serializing sql' or 'not implemented' rather than the explicit disabled message. The stub also has an unused receiver and parameter names in TablesList. Consider making the disable explicit at NewSQLCommand/Execute too, so every path reports the same reason.

false_positives.candidate:
Module checksums moved between go.sum and go.work.sum without a clear reason

The diff removes checksum lines for apache/thrift, klauspost/asmfmt, JohnCGriffin/overflow and others from go.sum and adds them to go.work.sum. Those modules are removed from go.mod as indirect dependencies, so the moves are inconsistent with the stated change. Running `go mod tidy` and `go work sync` should be verified so the checksum files match the module graph and the build is reproducible.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the BuildIndex-wide lock allows duplicate concurrent builds of the same key

BuildIndex previously held b.cacheMu for the whole build, serializing builds. Now the lock is only taken around the final map write. Two callers that miss the cache for the same NamespacedResource (for example a Search request via getOrCreateIndex racing with a watch event handled by handleEvent, or init racing with either) will both run the full build. For file-backed indexes (size > FileThreshold), bleve.New on the same directory will fail for the second caller, or the two indexes will each be built and one silently overwrites the other in b.cache, leaking an open bleve index. The fix needs per-key singleflight or a check-again under lock before building, not just finer locking around the cache write.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs iterates the cache map without holding cacheMu

TotalDocs ranges over b.cache with no lock, while BuildIndex now writes to b.cache under cacheMu. Concurrent map read and write is a data race and can crash the process with 'concurrent map iteration and map write'. TotalDocs is called from searchSupport.init for logging. The read should take cacheMu.RLock().

false_positives.candidate:
Index build now blocks construction and can fail server startup without a timeout

Moving Init into NewResourceServer means the full index build (search.init, which walks every namespace/resource) now runs synchronously before the server is returned. Callers, including module startup, now block on that work and fail hard if any build errors, where previously the failure only surfaced on individual RPCs. The context passed is the unbounded background context with no deadline. The PR asks whether anything depended on lazy init. Callers that constructed the server and expected it to be cheap or to tolerate index failure are affected, and this needs to be called out and tested.

Partially initialized resources leak when Init fails in NewResourceServer

If s.Init returns an error, NewResourceServer returns nil without calling s.cancel() or Stop. The background context created earlier, and any watcher goroutines already started by initWatcher or search init, are never torn down. Since init now runs at construction time and can fail, the failure path should cancel the context and release lifecycle resources.

Postgres variant of the storage-server integration test is now skipped

The new skip for postgres means the only test that exercises the storage server target with a real database no longer runs for postgres in CI. The change is unrelated to the PR's stated goals (init, tracing, indexing speed) and reduces coverage of the startup path that this PR changes, with no linked issue tracking the re-enable.

Stop no longer gates RPCs, and initErr is written without synchronization

Previously every RPC called s.Init, which returned s.initErr, so calls after Stop returned 'service is stopping' or 'service is stopped'. The Init calls were removed from Read, List, Create, Update, Delete, Search, History, Origin, IsHealthy, PutBlob, GetBlob and Watch, so those errors are no longer returned after Stop. Stop also writes s.initErr without any lock while other goroutines may read it. Both are behavior changes that the PR does not mention.

init goroutines write shared variables without synchronization

Inside group.Go, the closure does `totalBatchesIndexed++` and `_, _, err = s.build(...)`. Both `totalBatchesIndexed` and the outer `err` are shared across the errgroup goroutines, so this is a data race on each increment and assignment. A failing build can also overwrite another goroutine's error, so group.Wait may return the wrong error. Use a local err variable inside the closure and an atomic counter.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup registers a literal "alias" instead of the created IDP alias

The cleanup `getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove)` uses the literal string "alias" rather than the alias of the IDP just created. The cleanup therefore never removes the `idp-alias-N` providers, so they leak into other tests in the same realm. The same copy-paste pattern also appears at line 425 for `idp-alias-20`. The method reference should capture the actual alias.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
getForLogin Javadoc does not describe the new public-broker requirement

The change adds `idp.getOrganizationId() == null || BROKER_PUBLIC` to `LoginFilter.getLoginPredicate()`, so an org-linked IDP now qualifies for login only if it is marked broker-public. The Javadoc for `getForLogin` (lines 150-158) still says an IDP is usable for login if it is enabled, not link-only, and not hidden on login. It omits this new condition, which callers and maintainers will need to know.

remove() now always loads the IDP from the database

`IdentityProviderModel storedIdp = idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias);` is executed unconditionally at the top of `remove()`. Previously the DB lookup only happened when the alias key was invalidated, and the cache path avoided it entirely. Every IDP removal now incurs an extra uncached DB query, even when the cached entry is present and could supply the same data for the login-invalidation check.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider returns the provider of a default KeyStore instance

The method creates a KeyStore of the default type and returns its Provider, which is not a BouncyCastle provider and is only the provider of an uninitialized keystore. Callers that expect BC (e.g. for registering or looking up BC algorithms) will get an unrelated provider, or the method may throw IllegalStateException on a misconfigured keystore type.

true_positives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
concatenatedRSToASN1DER computes encodings and discards them

Lines 114-115 create two ASN1Encoder instances, write r and s into them, and throw the results away. This is dead code that does redundant BigInteger encoding work on every signature conversion and suggests the encoding logic was not carefully reviewed.

true_positives.golden_comment: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
readSequence loop can run forever or misparse when element length is zero

In readSequence the loop subtracts bytes.length from the remaining length; readNext returns the full TLV including tag and length. If the decoder returns indefinite length (-1 from readLength) or a zero-length element, length never reaches zero and the loop can spin or read past the sequence. Indefinite length is not rejected here.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract method order() breaks all existing CryptoProvider implementations

order() is added as an abstract interface method with no default. Any third-party or other in-repo CryptoProvider implementation that does not override it will fail to compile. Providing a default would preserve compatibility.

false_positives.candidate:
Ignored providers logged via debugf with non-constant format string

logger.debugf(builder.toString()) passes the built string as a format pattern; any '%' in a class name or future text will be misinterpreted as a format specifier and throw or garble the message. Use debugf with a format argument.

Multiple providers no longer rejected, changing detection semantics silently

Previously multiple CryptoProvider implementations on the classpath caused an IllegalStateException. Now the highest-order one is silently chosen and the rest only logged at debug level. A misconfigured deployment with two providers of equal order gets an arbitrary pick (sort is stable but ServiceLoader order is not deterministic across classpaths) with no warning.

Provider order 100 ranks below DefaultCryptoProvider but most methods throw UnsupportedOperationException

CryptoIntegration now picks the highest order. This provider has order 100 while Default/Elytron/FIPS use 200, so it is chosen only when they are absent. But if it is selected (authz-client used standalone), every method other than getEcdsaCryptoProvider throws UnsupportedOperationException, including getKeyStore's siblings and createECParams, so any non-ECDSA path in the client fails at runtime.

Test only checks round trip of concatenated RS, not that DER is valid or matches the reference

The test asserts asn1derToConcatenatedRS(concatenatedRSToASN1DER(x)) equals x, but never verifies the produced DER against the original signature or checks signature verification succeeds. A symmetric bug in both directions would pass. It should verify the signature with the converted DER and cover edge cases such as leading-zero/high-bit components.

concatenatedRSToASN1DER builds r and s with a forced leading zero byte, producing non-minimal and wrong integers

The method copies each half of the signature into an array of length len+1 with a leading 0 byte, then calls new BigInteger(r). That is always non-negative, which is correct for the sign, but the DER encoding then writes BigInteger.toByteArray() of the value, which is minimal. The only real issue is that signLength/2 is assumed equal to each component length; for odd or mismatched signLength inputs the arraycopy silently misbehaves or throws ArrayIndexOutOfBounds instead of an IOException. Also the method is not used by the ECDSA verification path in the test, so the round-trip test covers only the happy path.

readInteger drops the sign-extension semantics needed for ECDSA components and does not check length

readInteger reads the content with read(length) and builds BigInteger(bytes) without validating that length is positive or that the value is non-negative. ECDSA r/s values from a malicious or malformed DER signature can be arbitrarily large or negative; integerToBytes then truncates them silently, so a signature with out-of-range components can be mapped to a different valid-looking concatenated value instead of being rejected.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Listener gated on V1 feature flag, silently disabling cleanup for V2

The whole listener body is now wrapped in Profile.isFeatureEnabled(ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ). Previously it ran unconditionally. Under V2 (where only ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 may be enabled), role, client and group removal no longer clean up permission state. This behavior change is unrelated to adding clients and is not explained in the PR.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Possible NullPointerException when the 'all clients' resource is missing

In hasPermission(ClientModel, scope), if no per-client resource exists, the code loads the Clients type resource via getResourceTypeResource(). That method returns null when the schema is unsupported or the resource is not found. The result is passed straight to getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource) without a null check, which can throw an NPE instead of returning false.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

false_positives.candidate:
Client-removed listener calls V2 setPermissionsEnabled, which always throws

The ClientRemovedEvent branch calls management(...).clients().setPermissionsEnabled(client, false). With ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 enabled, management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2, whose clients() now returns ClientPermissionsV2. Its setPermissionsEnabled unconditionally throws UnsupportedOperationException. Deleting any client in a realm under V2 can therefore fail or leave the realm in a half-deleted state.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance
Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:

false_positives.candidate:
Feature name hardcoded in message instead of derived from the enum

printFeatureDisabled hardcodes the string 'rolling-updates'. The feature key is available as Profile.Feature.ROLLING_UPDATES.getKey(), so if the key is ever renamed the message will silently diverge from the actual flag. The same literal is also duplicated in the test assertion and in the docs.

Overwrites user-configured enabled features in the test deployment

createInitialDeployment calls setEnabledFeatures(List.of(ROLLING_UPDATES)) unconditionally on the FeatureSpec. If getTestKeycloakDeployment or a caller already set enabled features, they are replaced rather than merged, so the test base configuration can be silently dropped and the test no longer exercises what it was written to exercise.

Recreate exit code silently changed from 4 to 3

RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE changes from 4 to 3, and the new FEATURE_DISABLED takes 4. The update-compatibility command is documented as a scriptable, CI/CD-facing interface whose exit code is the contract. Any pipeline that already branches on exit code 4 for 'recreate required' will now treat it as 'feature disabled' and take the wrong action. The PR gives no rationale for renumbering an existing code instead of appending a new one. The comment about picocli ExitCode does not justify the value 3 either.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission collects resource names as IDs via findByType on the Groups type

In the V2 override, the granted IDs are added using groupResource.getId() (the Resource UUID), but the caller expects group IDs (the V1 implementation used resource name suffix). Group resources in V2 are typically named after the group id via the 'all-groups' type resource, so the stored value is the Resource entity id, not the group id. Callers (UserPermissions/UsersResource count and search) pass these to session.setAttribute(UserModel.GROUPS) and getUsersCount, which expect group model ids; the result will silently match no groups, so non-admin users with group-based VIEW_MEMBERS will see no members.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.

false_positives.candidate:
Inconsistent use of group.getId() vs resource names for group lookup in canView/canManage

hasPermission(group.getId(), ...) calls resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId). Group resources in this PR are created by the schema with the group id as name (see AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup/getOrCreateResource), but GroupPermissions (V1) uses a 'group.resource.' prefix; any V2 group resource not yet created will fall through to the all-groups check and may grant access via the type-level permission without a per-group resource, which is intended but untested for the view path.

No test covers view of group members through GroupResource.getMembers or getSubGroups filtering

The new group-resource tests cover update/create/view listing, but never verify that a user with VIEW_MEMBERS can list members via /groups/{id}/members or that subgroup filtering in GroupResource.getSubGroups honours per-group view permissions after the canView(g) change. The regression risk from the removed canViewGlobal shortcut is untested.

canManage/canView/canMapRoles pass group-check results but canMapRoles in V2 now ignores MAP_ROLES semantics for group members

canMapRoles in V2 now grants access when the user has MANAGE on the user or manage-members on a group, and the MAP_ROLES scope check is combined with MANAGE in a single OR. This broadens who can map roles compared to the previous MAP_ROLES-only check, a security-relevant permission widening that is not covered by any test in the PR.

canViewByGroup now calls groups().canViewMembers, changing V1 semantics and recursion through hierarchy

canViewByGroup previously used getGroupsWithViewPermission(group) which returned true for users with view-users roles and checked VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS. It now delegates to canViewMembers, which itself returns true when root.users().canView(), causing redundant evaluation per group for every user in the stream filter, a performance regression on large user searches (each user triggers permission evaluation across its whole group hierarchy).

canViewMembers/canManageMembers in V2 skip the group-independent MANAGE/VIEW fallback semantics and ignore user-level path

canViewMembers(group) only checks VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS on the group or all-groups resource. The V1 contract and the Javadoc in GroupPermissionEvaluator say a caller with MANAGE on the group should also view members; V2 canManageMembership checks MANAGE but canViewMembers does not, so behavior is inconsistent with the documented interface.

getOrCreateResource switch without a default for null resourceType handled inconsistently

The switch on resourceType will throw NullPointerException if resourceType is null (switch on a null String), instead of the explicit IllegalStateException used for unknown types. Callers passing a null type from a malformed request will get a 500 instead of a validation error.

hasPermission looks up resources by groupId as a resource name, but group resources are named by group id differently and falls back to type resource incorrectly

resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId) is used to find the group's resource, yet the 'all-groups' fallback uses getResourceTypeResource(...) and then checks policyStore.findByResource(server, resource). If the type resource is null (schema not initialized for the realm), resource.getScopes() / evaluatePermission will throw NPE at line 152 because resource is dereferenced without a null check on the fallback path.

true_positives.golden_comment: The translation is in Italian instead of Lithuanian. This should be translated to Lithuanian to match the file's locale (messages_lt.properties).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Lithuanian totpStep1 replaced with untranslated Italian text

The new value 'Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:' is Italian, not Lithuanian, so Lithuanian users will see a foreign-language instruction. The string should be translated or the original kept.

true_positives.golden_comment: The anchor sanitization logic has a potential issue where it consumes English matcher groups without proper validation. If the translated text has more anchor tags than the English text, this could lead to incorrect validation results.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Anchor validation compares tags pairwise without checking counts or using the replaced value consistently

santizeAnchors walks anchors in the translation and in English with two independent matchers, and removes the matched English anchor text from value via replaceFirst on the translation. If the translation has more anchors than English, englishMatcher.find() fails and the message is added, but if it has fewer, extra English anchors are never reported. Also replaceFirst with a quoted pattern removes the first occurrence in value, which may not be the anchor just matched, so the check can pass or fail based on text position rather than structure.

true_positives.golden_comment: Field HTML_TAGS should be declared as 'private static final' following Java naming conventions for constants
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Policy factories are instance fields with non-private visibility and the HTML_TAGS pattern is package-private

POLICY_SOME_HTML, POLICY_NO_HTML and HTML_TAGS are declared without modifiers at package level, while sibling constants are private static. This is inconsistent and makes them mutable from the package; they should be static final to avoid rebuilding policies per instance.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The totpStep1 value uses Traditional Chinese terms in the Simplified Chinese file (zh_CN), which is likely incorrect for this locale. Please verify the locale‑appropriate translation.
The method name 'santizeAnchors' should be 'sanitizeAnchors' (missing 'i').

false_positives.candidate:
Czech error-invalid-multivalued-size message uses choice format with unexpected plural rules

The added choice pattern uses 1<hodnoty|4<hodnot which is a Czech plural rule that may not match Czech grammar for the value 2-4 (should be 'hodnoty'), so counts 2-4 render with the wrong form.

Dutch emailVerificationBodyHtml contains a malformed closing tag The line was changed from '

' ... '

U kunt' to '' which is a malformed tag, making the HTML body render incorrectly.

English file path derivation is fragile and can produce wrong or nonexistent paths

The English counterpart path is computed with regex replaceAll on the absolute path: replaceAll("resources-community", "resources") then replaceAll("_[a-zA-Z-_]*\\.properties", "_en.properties"). Any directory containing an underscore or the substring 'resources-community' elsewhere in the path, or a file without a locale suffix, will be rewritten incorrectly. When the English file is missing a RuntimeException is thrown, aborting verification for the whole module rather than reporting a message.

Fixture contains an unclosed tag that is also used as the English source

The fixture 'key=Some <div>tag</div' is malformed (missing '>'). The test asserts an 'Illegal HTML' message, but the failure may be caused by the malformed syntax rather than the intended illegal tag, so the test does not verify what its name says.

Hungarian emailUpdateConfirmationBodyHtml key prefixed with *** corrupting the key name

The line was changed to start with '***emailUpdateConfirmationBodyHtml=', so the property key is now '***emailUpdateConfirmationBodyHtml' and the real key is no longer translated. The HTML email body falls back to English or is missing.

Keys present only in the translation are checked against an empty English value, and missing English file throws

getEnglishValue returns "" for keys missing in English, so the sanitizer decides HTML policy from an empty string and silently accepts whatever HTML the translation contains for keys that do not exist in the source. Additionally, a missing English file is converted into a RuntimeException rather than a MojoExecutionException, so the plugin crashes with an unhelpful stack trace instead of a verification message.

Lithuanian email anchors changed to invalid href=LT"..." syntax

Several anchors were changed from href="{0}" to href=LT"{0}" (missing the opening quote before LT), producing broken attributes in verification and password-reset emails and in the executeActions email. Links in these emails will not work.

Lithuanian loginTotpStep1 replaced with Italian text

Same problem as the account bundle: the value is an Italian sentence, so the Lithuanian login page shows untranslated content.

Multivalued size message now uses choice format that the admin UI does not parse with the same placeholder

The message changed from value(s) to a choice format but the admin UI in js/apps uses {{0}} style placeholders for this key elsewhere; mixing styles risks the key rendering literally in the admin console.

Persian emailUpdateConfirmationBodyHtml change removes the space before a closing tag only by corrupting the markup

The original contained '< p>' malformed tag which was corrected, but this is a content-unrelated fix bundled into a sanitizer PR; unrelated edits make review of the real intent harder.

Slovak error-invalid-multivalued-size fix mixes change to plural form key The new value uses {2,choice,...} for the second placeholder and fixes {1} to {2} for the maximum, which is a correct fix, but the trailing newline removal and reordering in the same file was not needed for the sanitizer change; the bundle also keeps impersonateTitleHtml with a stray closing removed, changing markup unrelated to the PR.

Tests rely on fixtures whose English counterparts are not present and do not cover the passing path

The new tests call verify() on *_de.properties fixtures, but the English path derivation resolves to *_en.properties in the same directory; the tests never assert that a valid translation produces no messages, nor that a correct anchor passes. The duplicate-key test was relaxed from Matchers.contains to hasItem, weakening the assertion so extra unexpected messages go undetected.

Translated instruction text replaces the link-bearing content with a generic sentence that drops the app names

The totpStep1 string is changed to a generic sentence, removing the FreeOTP and Google Authenticator references and links. This is an unrelated content change to a translation file that loses information users need to set up OTP. It appears to be a side effect of the sanitizer change rather than an intended translation fix.

Turkish identityProviderLinkBodyHtml changed whitespace inside tags and made the anchor unbalanced The closing tags were changed from '' to '' and ' {1} ' spacing was altered; while '' is not valid HTML, the changes are unrelated to sanitization and break rendering of the email.

Unescaping HTML entities after sanitization can reintroduce unsafe markup in the comparison

sanitized = unescapeHtml4(sanitized) runs after the policy sanitizer. The comparison therefore accepts values in which entities such as <script> were decoded back into raw tags in the 'sanitized' string, and the check only flags a difference when the sanitized and original differ. Since value was also unescaped in normalizeValue, a translation containing '<img onerror=...>' is unescaped to a real tag before sanitizing, so the sanitizer does see it; but the post-sanitize unescape can turn entities the sanitizer intentionally kept into tags that the policy would reject, making the verifier's pass/fail result unreliable.

true_positives.golden_comment: In AccessTokenContext constructor, the fourth Objects.requireNonNull validates grantType twice instead of validating rawTokenId, allowing null rawTokenId values to pass validation.

Blank line removed while adding grant type attribute

The edit removes a blank line and inserts setAttribute in its place, which is cosmetic, but the attribute is set after the note and before the client is set; fine. Minor: no functional issue, included only as the diff replaced a blank line.

Cast of getProviderFactory result may throw ClassCastException

sessionFactory.getProviderFactory(OAuth2GrantType.class, grantType) returns a ProviderFactory that is cast directly to OAuth2GrantTypeFactory without checking; a non-OAuth2GrantTypeFactory implementation would fail at token issuance.

Grant type taken from context.getGrantType() which is the raw form parameter

context.getGrantType() returns the raw grant_type form parameter, which may be an arbitrary attacker-controlled string. It is stored as the grant type and, if it does not match a registered shortcut, encodeTokenId throws, causing a 500 instead of a proper OAuth error. Validation should happen before use.

Refresh grant type set after the original grant type was lost; overrides initial value for refreshed tokens

validateToken sets GRANT_TYPE to refresh_token on the client session context, but this is only applied on the refresh path. Other paths (e.g. the RefreshTokenGrantType itself, which does not call createTokenResponse) rely on this implicit setting, so the encoded grant in tokens depends on which code path ran, making the encoded grant type inconsistent.

Token ID encoding can throw during token issuance for unregistered grant types

initToken calls encoder.encodeTokenId, which throws IllegalStateException when the grant type has no registered shortcut (e.g. a grant set on clientSessionCtx that is not an OAuth2GrantType factory, or tokens created by other paths that never set GRANT_TYPE, where the default 'na' is used). Token creation now fails for flows that previously worked, rather than falling back to a plain id.

Token ID parsing throws on any non-encoded id containing ':' with wrong length

getTokenContextFromTokenId splits on the first ':' and throws IllegalArgumentException if the prefix is not exactly 6 chars. Any token id from a non-standard source (or a raw UUID with a colon, or legacy formats) causes an exception rather than falling back to UNKNOWN as done for ids without ':'. Callers (introspection, userinfo) that receive such ids will fail with 500 instead of degrading gracefully.

Token type derived from request-wide client attribute, not from the token being created

getShouldUseLightweightToken(session) reads session.getContext().getClient(), which is the requesting client, not necessarily the client the token is issued for (e.g. token exchange to another audience, or refresh flows), and the token mapper logic uses the same helper. The encoded token type may not match the actual token format produced, making the encoded context unreliable for the stated use (lightweight detection).

Unsynchronized lazy refresh of shared maps on every miss

getShortcutByGrantType and getGrantTypeByShortcut mutate the shared ConcurrentHashMaps during token issuance and token id parsing. The grantsByShortcuts/grantsToShortcuts maps are also written without any atomicity across the two maps, so concurrent readers can see them inconsistent. Also, an attacker-supplied unknown shortcut in a token id triggers a full stream scan of provider factories on every request (no negative caching), a cheap DoS amplification.

postInit throws on duplicate shortcuts but init/postInit use non-thread-safe HashMap for shortcut tables

The shortcut validation compares map sizes, which only detects duplicate shortcuts that collide with the same key; if two grants share a shortcut, one silently overwrites the other in grantsByShortcuts and the sizes still differ only by accident. The size check is an indirect and incomplete duplicate detection. Also OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.getShortcut() has no default, so third-party grant factories break at compile/startup.

false_positives.candidate:
Recovery codes are written to user storage in plaintext

createRecoveryCodesCredential serializes the raw generatedCodes list to JSON and passes it as the credential data to user.credentialManager().updateCredential(). The local-storage path instead stores a RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel built from the same codes, which is designed to hold hashed codes (RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode exists for this). External user storage providers therefore receive and persist usable plaintext recovery codes, which a storage backend or anyone with read access to it can use to bypass MFA. The test provider also has no test asserting that a used code is rejected, so this gap is not caught. The provider's contract should require consuming the code, or the code should be documented as a limitation.

Removal of exhausted codes does not work for user-storage credentials

false_positives.candidate:
--flusher-processes defaults to 1, so the PR's one-process-per-shard behavior is not the default

The new `--flusher-processes` option defaults to 1, and the factory forwards that value as `max_processes`. `SpanFlusher` then runs `min(max_processes, len(shards))` processes, so with the default every shard in the consumer is flushed by a single process. The PR description says the flusher should spawn a process per redis shard, but that only happens when operators pass a higher value explicitly. Either the default should be unset/None (meaning one process per shard) or the description and help text should say the default is a single process.

Hung thread-based flushers are restarted without being stopped

In `_ensure_processes_alive`, `process.kill()` is only called for `multiprocessing.Process`. For the `threading.Thread` path (used in tests with `produce_to_pipe`), a hung thread is left running and a second thread for the same shards is started. Both then flush the same buffer. This is limited to the test path, but it means restart behavior differs between modes.

A failing build can also overwrite another goroutine's error, so group.Wait may return the wrong error. Use a local err variable inside the closure and an atomic counter.

If s.Init returns an error, NewResourceServer returns nil without calling s.cancel() or Stop. The background context created earlier, and any watcher goroutines already started by initWatcher or search init, are never torn down. Since init now runs at construction time and can fail, the failure path should cancel the context and release lifecycle resources.

The context passed is the unbounded background context with no deadline. The PR asks whether anything depended on lazy init. Callers that constructed the server and expected it to be cheap or to tolerate index failure are affected, and this needs to be called out and tested.

false_positives.candidate:
Shared queue pool is shut down when a rebalance closes the old strategy

`create_thread_queue_parallel_worker` hands the same `self.queue_pool` to every strategy it creates, and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()`/`terminate()` (queue_consumer.py ~lines 335-342) call `queue_pool.shutdown()`. On a Kafka rebalance, arroyo calls `create_with_partitions` again and closes the previous strategy. The old strategy's close shuts down the pool that the new strategy is using. Afterwards `FixedQueuePool.submit` calls `queue.put` on shut-down queues, which raises, and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` logs and silently drops the message while marking its offset complete. Result messages are lost after any rebalance. The pool lifetime needs to be owned by the factory, not by each strategy's close().

Offsets are committed from a background thread, not the processing thread

`_commit_loop` runs in its own thread and calls `self.commit_function(committable)`, which is the arroyo `commit` callable bound to the consumer. Arroyo/Kafka consumer commits are not designed to be called concurrently with the consumer's poll loop from another thread, and the strategy's `poll()`/`submit()` run on the processing thread. This can race with the consumer's own commit/poll or with rebalance handling and produce undefined commit behaviour. Commits should be triggered from the strategy's poll/submit path on the processing thread.

A single missing offset permanently stalls commits for the partition

In `get_committable_offsets`, the loop breaks at the first offset that is not in `all_offsets`. Kafka offsets are not guaranteed contiguous (log compaction, transaction control markers, aborted transactions). If an offset is never delivered to `submit`, `highest_committable` never advances past it, and every later offset is treated as blocked forever. Consumer lag then grows without bound and the committed position never moves, so on restart everything after the gap is reprocessed. The tracker should treat the gap as a non-outstanding position, e.g. by advancing over offsets that were never registered and were below the next delivered offset.

Queues are unbounded, so the advertised backpressure does not exist

The class docstring claims 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but every queue is created with `queue.Queue()` (no maxsize), and `submit` never blocks. The consumer will keep polling and buffering Kafka messages in memory whenever a slow worker falls behind, which can exhaust memory under a backlog. Either bound the queues and block or pause the consumer, or remove the claim from the docstring.

Shutdown discards queued work items without draining them

`FixedQueuePool.shutdown` sets `worker.shutdown = True` before shutting down the queues. The worker loop checks that flag before each `get`, so items still queued are abandoned rather than processed. Their offsets are never committed, so they will be reprocessed later. This is safe for at-least-once delivery, but it is not what the 'no item is lost' guarantee in the strategy docstring implies, and nothing logs how many items were dropped.

All factory tests create one strategy per factory and shut the factory down at the end. There is no test that calls `create_with_partitions` twice, closes the first strategy, and then submits to the second. Such a test would expose that closing one strategy shuts down the shared queue pool and drops messages.

Post.cook returns raw when cook_method is raw_html, so remote content (RSS items or fetched pages via Readability, which is only partially whitelisted and not applied to feed content) is rendered unsanitized into the forum and served to readers, enabling stored XSS from any imported feed.

Adding force: true makes the migration drop and recreate the top_topics table if it already exists, destroying any existing rows. Migrations that have already run are unaffected, but on a DB where the table exists this silently wipes data.

The response assertions are in an after block, so they run after each example rather than as part of it, and the tests are not checking the rendered behaviour for the loading case. Failures are reported confusingly and the 404 test does not verify the status.

The startTime/endTime are computed as `hour()*60 + minute()` after shifting by the timezone offset, which discards the date. Keys present only in the translation are checked against an empty English value, and missing English file throws

getTokenContextFromTokenId splits on the first ':' and throws IllegalArgumentException if the prefix is not exactly 6 chars. Any token id from a non-standard source (or a raw UUID with a colon, or legacy formats) causes an exception rather than falling back to UNKNOWN as done for ids without ':'. Callers (introspection, userinfo) that receive such ids will fail with 500 instead of degrading gracefully.

Token type derived from request-wide client attribute, not from the token being created

getShouldUseLightweightToken(session) reads session.getContext().getClient(), which is the requesting client, not necessarily the client the token is issued for (e.g. token exchange to another audience, or refresh flows), and the token mapper logic uses the same helper. The encoded token type may not match the actual token format produced, making the encoded context unreliable for the stated use (lightweight detection).

Unsynchronized lazy refresh of shared maps on every miss

getShortcutByGrantType and getGrantTypeByShortcut mutate the shared ConcurrentHashMaps during token issuance and token id parsing. The grantsByShortcuts/grantsToShortcuts maps are also written without any atomicity across the two maps, so concurrent readers can see them inconsistent. Also, an attacker-supplied unknown shortcut in a token id triggers a full stream scan of provider factories on every request (no negative caching), a cheap DoS amplification.

postInit throws on duplicate shortcuts but init/postInit use non-thread-safe HashMap for shortcut tables

The shortcut validation compares map sizes, which only detects duplicate shortcuts that collide with the same key; if two grants share a shortcut, one silently overwrites the other in grantsByShortcuts and the sizes still differ only by accident. The size check is an indirect and incomplete duplicate detection. Also OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.getShortcut() has no default, so third-party grant factories break at compile/startup.

Cast of getProviderFactory result may throw ClassCastException

sessionFactory.getProviderFactory(OAuth2GrantType.class, grantType) returns a ProviderFactory that is cast directly to OAuth2GrantTypeFactory without checking; a non-OAuth2GrantTypeFactory implementation would fail at token issuance.

Token ID encoding can throw during token issuance for unregistered grant types

initToken calls encoder.encodeTokenId, which throws IllegalStateException when the grant type has no registered shortcut (e.g. a grant set on clientSessionCtx that is not an OAuth2GrantType factory, or tokens created by other paths that never set GRANT_TYPE, where the default 'na' is used). Token creation now fails for flows that previously worked, rather than falling back to a plain id.

Blank line removed while adding grant type attribute

The edit removes a blank line and inserts setAttribute in its place, which is cosmetic, but the attribute is set after the note and before the client is set; fine. Minor: no functional issue, included only as the diff replaced a blank line.

Refresh grant type set after the original grant type was lost; overrides initial value for refreshed tokens

validateToken sets GRANT_TYPE to refresh_token on the client session context, but this is only applied on the refresh path. Other paths (e.g. the RefreshTokenGrantType itself, which does not call createTokenResponse) rely on this implicit setting, so the encoded grant in tokens depends on which code path ran, making the encoded grant type inconsistent.

Grant type taken from context.getGrantType() which is the raw form parameter

context.getGrantType() returns the raw grant_type form parameter, which may be an arbitrary attacker-controlled string. It is stored as the grant type and, if it does not match a registered shortcut, encodeTokenId throws, causing a 500 instead of a proper OAuth error. Validation should happen before use.

updateCredential assigns a generated id to recoveryCodesModel, but getCredentials rebuilds the model with RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues(...), which does not copy that id. true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that rebuilding the recovery-code credential model fails to preserve the stored credential ID, leaving getId() null and preventing downstream removal by ID.

false_positives.candidate:
Recovery codes are written to user storage in plaintext

createRecoveryCodesCredential serializes the raw generatedCodes list to JSON and passes it as the credential data to user.credentialManager().updateCredential(). The local-storage path instead stores a RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel built from the same codes, which is designed to hold hashed codes (RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode exists for this). External user storage providers therefore receive and persist usable plaintext recovery codes, which a storage backend or anyone with read access to it can use to bypass MFA. The user-storage branch should store hashed codes, matching the local representation, and verification should compare hashes.

Recovery codes in user storage are never consumed after use

isValid for RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE only checks membership in the stored list and never removes or marks the used code. In local storage each code is single-use, so a code entered once can be entered again here indefinitely. The test provider also has no test asserting that a used code is rejected, so this gap is not caught. The provider's contract should require consuming the code, or the code should be documented as a limitation.

Removal of exhausted codes does not work for user-storage credentials

getCredential now returns federated (user storage) credentials first, but the removal call at line 86 uses credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(), which only operates on local-storage credentials. When the exhausted codes come from user storage, nothing is removed. The exhausted credential stays in storage, and getCredential keeps finding it on later logins. The removal should go through a path that handles federated credentials, or the mismatch should be handled explicitly.

RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE changes from 4 to 3, and the new FEATURE_DISABLED takes 4. The update-compatibility command is documented as a scriptable, CI/CD-facing interface whose exit code is the contract. Any pipeline that already branches on exit code 4 for 'recreate required' will now treat it as 'feature disabled' and take the wrong action. The PR gives no rationale for renumbering an existing code instead of appending a new one. The comment about picocli ExitCode does not justify the value 3 either.

printFeatureDisabled hardcodes the string 'rolling-updates'. The feature key is available as Profile.Feature.ROLLING_UPDATES.getKey(), so if the key is ever renamed the message will silently diverge from the actual flag. The same literal is also duplicated in the test assertion and in the docs.

createInitialDeployment calls setEnabledFeatures(List.of(ROLLING_UPDATES)) unconditionally on the FeatureSpec. If getTestKeycloakDeployment or a caller already set enabled features, they are replaced rather than merged, so the test base configuration can be silently dropped and the test no longer exercises what it was written to exercise.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

Under V2 (where only ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 may be enabled), role, client and group removal no longer clean up permission state. This behavior change is unrelated to adding clients and is not explained in the PR.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the listener being incorrectly gated by the V1 feature flag, preventing permission cleanup for role, client, and group removals when only V2 is enabled and leaving orphaned permissions.

The result is passed straight to getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource) without a null check, which can throw an NPE instead of returning false.

With ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 enabled, management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2, whose clients() now returns ClientPermissionsV2. Its setPermissionsEnabled unconditionally throws UnsupportedOperationException. Deleting any client in a realm under V2 can therefore fail or leave the realm in a half-deleted state.

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission collects resource names as IDs via findByType on the Groups type

In the V2 override, the granted IDs are added using groupResource.getId() (the Resource UUID), but the caller expects group IDs (the V1 implementation used resource name suffix). Group resources in V2 are typically named after the group id via the 'all-groups' type resource, so the stored value is the Resource entity id, not the group id. The candidate does not explicitly discuss hasPermission's name-based resolution, but captures the central bug and its filtering consequences.

hasPermission looks up resources by groupId as a resource name, but group resources are named by group id differently and falls back to type resource incorrectly

resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId) is used to find the group's resource, yet the 'all-groups' fallback uses getResourceTypeResource(...) and then checks policyStore.findByResource(server, resource). If the type resource is null (schema not initialized for the realm), resource.getScopes() / evaluatePermission will throw NPE at line 152 because resource is dereferenced without a null check on the fallback path.

canViewMembers(group) only checks VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS on the group or all-groups resource. The V1 contract and the Javadoc in GroupPermissionEvaluator say a caller with MANAGE on the group should also view members; V2 canManageMembership checks MANAGE but canViewMembers does not, so behavior is inconsistent with the documented interface.

It now delegates to canViewMembers, which itself returns true when root.users().canView(), causing redundant evaluation per group for every user in the stream filter, a performance regression on large user searches (each user triggers permission evaluation across its whole group hierarchy).

canManage/canView/canMapRoles pass group-check results but canMapRoles in V2 now ignores MAP_ROLES semantics for group members

canMapRoles in V2 now grants access when the user has MANAGE on the user or manage-members on a group, and the MAP_ROLES scope check is combined with MANAGE in a single OR. This broadens who can map roles compared to the previous MAP_ROLES-only check, a security-relevant permission widening that is not covered by any test in the PR.

Inconsistent use of group.getId() vs resource names for group lookup in canView/canManage

hasPermission(group.getId(), ...) calls resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId). Group resources in this PR are created by the schema with the group id as name (see AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup/getOrCreateResource), but GroupPermissions (V1) uses a 'group.resource.' prefix; any V2 group resource not yet created will fall through to the all-groups check and may grant access via the type-level permission without a per-group resource, which is intended but untested for the view path.

No test covers view of group members through GroupResource.getMembers or getSubGroups filtering

The new group-resource tests cover update/create/view listing, but never verify that a user with VIEW_MEMBERS can list members via /groups/{id}/members or that subgroup filtering in GroupResource.getSubGroups honours per-group view permissions after the canView(g) change. The regression risk from the removed canViewGlobal shortcut is untested.

getOrCreateResource switch without a default for null resourceType handled inconsistently

The switch on resourceType will throw NullPointerException if resourceType is null (switch on a null String), instead of the explicit IllegalStateException used for unknown types. Callers passing a null type from a malformed request will get a 500 instead of a validation error.

This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. The cache key embeds hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids))). Python's hash() for ints is deterministic, but the tuple hash is not guaranteed stable across processes and can collide; a collision would return another project set's eligibility for this org. The key also ignores that eligibility depends on the allowlist option, so a stale value can persist for 60s. Use the sorted project ids joined as a string instead.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same concern: using Python's hash() for project-based cache keys may produce inconsistent keys across processes, and recommends deterministic serialization of sorted project IDs. The additional collision and allowlist concerns do not negate the match.

Cached eligibility is returned without re-checking, and cache.get of False is treated as hit

The cache stores is_eligible and the cached path returns cached_result and transform check. This is consistent, but the cache is keyed only by org and project ids, not by the dataset/request, and the allowlist is also re-read fresh elsewhere, so the 'fresh' docstring contradicts the caching added in this PR. Behavior differs between cache hit and miss within the 60s window, producing inconsistent results for identical queries.

project_id in allowlist assumes the option stores integer ids. If the option is stored as strings (common for options edited via UI/JSON), no project matches and upsampling silently never applies; if types mismatch in the other direction, the check fails silently. The membership test should normalize types.

The transform replaces count() with an aliased function call regardless of whether the query's orderby, equations, or top-events column references 'count()'. Callers that look up the result by 'count()' key or pass the transformed columns into equations/orderby will break. The alias 'count' also may collide with a user-specified column of the same name.

The function assumes sample_weight exists for every event in allowlisted projects, but events without the context (for example, older SDKs or events stored before the change) have no sample_weight, so sum() undercounts them to zero or fails the query. The comment asserts a schema guarantee that the code does not enforce. The function also declares required_args=[] and default_result_type 'number' while it is used as an aggregate with the toInt64 wrapper, which truncates fractional sample weights.

is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects is invoked at the top of _get_event_stats, which is called multiple times per request (split-query flow, transaction queries). The response detail for topEvents <= 0 changed from 'If topEvents needs to be at least 1' to 'topEvents needs to be at least 1'. This is an unrelated behavior change in an upsampling PR that may break clients or tests matching the old string.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The usual fix is to re-read the cache after acquiring the write lock and return early if it is already populated. This only matters at startup or in dev mode, so the impact is limited to redundant file reads and parsing.

A slow or hung CDN request, bounded only by the context, can stall all page renders. Consider doing the load outside the lock and only publishing the result under the lock.
