BlockedEmail.where(email: email) compares the raw string. User emails are downcased via Email.downcase elsewhere in the codebase, and the blocked_emails table stores whatever was entered. An entry 'Bad@Spam.com' will not block 'bad@spam.com', so blocking is trivially bypassed.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify case-sensitive email matching in BlockedEmail as allowing blocked users to bypass a block by changing email capitalization. The reversed capitalization example describes the same underlying bug.

false_positives.candidate:
Blocked-email check is applied to any attribute using the validator

The validator is generic (ActiveModel::EachValidator) but the blocked-email lookup runs unconditionally, and the error key is hardcoded to user.email.blocked. Any future use on other attributes will apply the block list and misreport. Also the not_allowed/blocked messages are added to attribute, fine, but the check is coupled to User semantics.

Returning user attributes and raw errors in the create response leaks data

The failure response now includes values from user.attributes.slice('name','username','email') and the full errors hash. This echoes submitted data back and exposes validation detail (including the blocked-email signal) to unauthenticated callers, which lets anonymous users probe whether an email is blocked via the 'is not allowed.' error, bypassing the generic message.

rejectedEmails is populated from result.values.email, which may be undefined

pushObject(result.values.email) is guarded only by result.values being truthy. If the server omits email (e.g. the field is absent), undefined is pushed, and the email check then never matches the real address. The entry is also never removed, so a user who corrects a typo stays blocked only for the rejected string, but a legitimately fixed email is still validated correctly; the main issue is the undefined push and unbounded growth of the array.

Unique index without a case-normalized value and no email format constraint

The unique index on email is case-sensitive, so the same address in different cases can be stored twice, and only one of them would be matched by the case-sensitive lookup. Normalization should happen at write time or in the index expression.

Validator spec does not test the whitelist/blacklist behavior it moved

The User email_validator and email_in_restriction_setting? logic was moved into EmailValidator, but the new spec only covers blocked emails. Regressions in the whitelist/blacklist domain checks are not caught. The spec also stubs should_block? so the side-effect bug above is never exercised.

No test for uniqueness, case handling, or save failure

The spec does not verify the uniqueness validation or case-insensitive matching, and does not verify that validation (not just should_block?) leaves match_count unchanged. The 'updates statistics' expectation passes while the validator incorrectly increments counts on each User validation.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

true_positives.golden_comment: Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`.panel` float removed and replaced with flex ordering without verification

`.panel` changes from `float: right` to `margin-left: auto` plus `order(3)`. This only works if `.panel` is a direct flex child of `.contents`. If it is nested under another wrapper, the float is removed with no equivalent layout, and the header can shift in ways the PR does not account for.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the loss of right alignment when .panel's float is replaced with flex-based styling but .panel is nested in a wrapper rather than being a direct flex item. The candidate describes the same layout regression without naming the non-Ember/noscript header specifically.

true_positives.golden_comment: -ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`align-items` mixin emits a non-existent `-ms-align-items` property

`-ms-align-items` is not a real vendor-prefixed property, so the declaration is dropped by browsers and is dead output. `-webkit-box-align` also accepts only box-model values, so the mixin is misleading for the flexbox intent. The mixin should emit only valid properties.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same core issue: the mixin emits the nonexistent -ms-align-items property. Although it does not name -ms-flex-align as the replacement and adds another concern, it matches the golden comment's underlying bug.

false_positives.candidate:
Removing the `.title` float rule may break the header title layout

The `.title { float: left; }` rule is deleted outright and nothing replaces it, while `.contents` becomes a flex container. Any header markup still using the `.title` class loses its float and will be positioned by flex rules it was never designed for. The PR does not show that the class is unused, so the header title layout is at risk.

Bullet badge margin rule removed from extra-info wrapper without replacement

The `&.bullet { margin-top: 5px; }` rule inside `.extra-info-wrapper .badge-wrapper` is deleted. Bullet badges in this wrapper lose their 5px top offset, which changes their vertical alignment. The diff also adds an unrelated `line-height: 1.5` to the same wrapper, which is not explained.

Small-action description spacing reduced without clear justification

`.small-action-desc` padding changes from `0.5em 0 0.5em 4em` to `0 1.5%`, the `margin-top: 5px` is dropped, and the nested `p` margin and padding are changed as well. The left indent of 4em that reserves room for the avatar is removed, so the text can overlap the `.topic-avatar` column. These are visible layout changes with no supporting description or test.

PR description is empty and the title does not match the changes

The description reads only 'Test 5', so reviewers get no rationale for the layout changes. The title claims a performance optimization, but the diff is a visual layout rewrite (float to flexbox, spacing and margin changes) with no measurements or verification of the intended behavior.

false_negatives.golden_comment: -webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.

false_positives.candidate:
website_name leaks the profile website to anonymous viewers of TL0 users

`:website_name` is added to the plain `attributes` list, but it is not added to the `untrusted_attributes` list (lines 105-111). `website`, `location`, `bio_raw` and `profile_background` are all hidden for TL0 users seen by anonymous visitors, via `scope.restrict_user_fields?`. `website_name` is derived directly from `website`, so for a TL0 user it is still serialized. Anonymous users can therefore see the website host, and with this change the full URL path, which the restriction was meant to hide. The TL0 spec (spec/serializers/user_serializer_spec.rb line 11) still lists only the old untrusted attributes, so it does not catch the leak. Fix: add `:website_name` to `untrusted_attributes` and extend the spec's list.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Referer host check is the only access control and is trivially spoofable

ensure_embeddable trusts request.referer to decide whether the embed endpoint may be served, and then sets X-Frame-Options to ALLOWALL. Referer headers are client-controlled and can be stripped or forged by non-browser clients, so any caller can fetch the embed page. Combined with ALLOWALL, the page can be framed from any origin. The check gates only on referer, not on a shared secret or origin validation.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same core security issue: setting X-Frame-Options to ALLOWALL disables framing protection, while relying on spoofable Referer headers does not provide effective validation. It omits the nil-referer fallback detail, but still matches the underlying vulnerability.

true_positives.golden_comment: The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
import mutates the caller's contents string and interpolates unescaped title/url into HTML

contents << ... modifies the string passed in by the caller (PollFeed passes i.content which is then reused), and the url is interpolated unescaped into an href inside HTML that is stored as raw_html and rendered without cooking, creating a stored XSS vector if the URL contains quotes. Since cook_method raw_html skips sanitization, feed content is stored and displayed verbatim.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same XSS vulnerability caused by interpolating an unescaped URL into generated HTML. It does not mention the nil-contents NoMethodError and adds a separate mutation concern, but it matches a core issue in the golden comment.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
i.content may be nil and scrub is called on it

SimpleRSS items without a content element return nil for i.content, so i.content.scrub raises NoMethodError and aborts the whole poll loop, skipping all remaining feed items.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: RSS items may lack content, so calling i.content.scrub on nil raises an exception. The candidate matches the underlying issue even though it does not suggest falling back to description.

true_positives.golden_comment: An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
request.referer interpolated into a JavaScript string literal

The referer is inserted into a script string without JavaScript escaping. A referer containing a quote or newline breaks out of the string and injects script. Use json or escape_javascript and validate the origin.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same XSS vulnerability: request.referer is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, allowing malicious header content to inject and execute scripts.

false_positives.candidate:
Anonymous requests enqueue retrieve jobs without throttle bypass and can trigger remote fetches

Every request to best without an existing TopicEmbed enqueues a retrieve_topic job with an arbitrary embed_url. TopicRetriever only throttles per URL via redis setnx, so an attacker can enumerate many distinct URLs on the embeddable host to cause unbounded remote HTTP fetches and job queue growth.

Port handling in absolutize_urls is wrong for non-default ports and scheme

prefix appends the port unless it is 80 or 443 regardless of scheme, and uri.port for an https URL on port 80 or http on 443 is wrongly dropped/kept. More importantly the prefix is built with string << on a fresh string each call, which is fine, but the scheme check is missing: URLs with other schemes are not constrained here. The main consequence is incorrect absolute links for some URL/port combinations.

Raw HTML from remote feeds/pages is stored with raw_html cook method, skipping sanitization

Post.cook returns raw when cook_method is raw_html, so remote content (RSS items or fetched pages via Readability, which is only partially whitelisted and not applied to feed content) is rendered unsanitized into the forum and served to readers, enabling stored XSS from any imported feed.

open() of a URL uses Kernel#open which can execute commands or read local files

open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) with a string relies on Kernel#open, which in older Ruby interprets pipe-prefixed strings as shell commands and otherwise reads local files. Use URI.open/open-uri explicitly or a safer fetch.

embeddable_host comparison is case sensitive and ignores port

invalid_host? compares SiteSetting.embeddable_host to URI(...).host exactly, so a host with different case (Eviltrout.com) is rejected, and the controller's referer check does the same. Inconsistent with browser host semantics and may reject valid embeds.

Disqus import now fetches each thread's remote page and discards the post's per-comment creation

The import replaces PostCreator creation of a permalink post with TopicEmbed.import_remote, which fetches the live page over HTTP. Dry-run and offline imports now depend on network access, and the blank line left behind plus the removed category option break the documented CLI interface (the -c option is removed without replacement).

cook_method check returns raw content without any escaping for all raw_html posts

cook short-circuits to return raw for raw_html posts, bypassing Plugin::Filter :after_post_cook hooks and any sanitization. Combined with cook being called in before_create_tasks, posts created this way are never filtered by plugins.

skip_validations now changes save behaviour for all revisions, and return value is ignored

update_post calls @post.save(validate: !@opts[:skip_validations]) and ignores the result. Previously the same save ran, but with validations skipped on imported posts, rate-limit and spam validations bypass is now possible; the failed save is also silently ignored, so revise! returns true even when the post failed to save.

force: true on create_table will drop existing top_topics data on migration

Adding force: true makes the migration drop and recreate the top_topics table if it already exists, destroying any existing rows. Migrations that have already run are unaffected, but on a DB where the table exists this silently wipes data.

Adding NOT NULL column with default to large posts table rewrites the table

add_column with default and null: false on Postgres of older versions rewrites the whole posts table under an exclusive lock, which can block a production forum for a long time.

Success assertions placed in after hook and error tests use weak checks

The response assertions are in an after block, so they run after each example rather than as part of it, and the tests are not checking the rendered behaviour for the loading case. Failures are reported confusingly and the 404 test does not verify the status.

Spec does not cover the update path's content_sha1 handling or the no-change case

The 'Supports updating the post' test does not assert the embed record's content_sha1 was updated nor that unchanged content skips revision, so regressions in the update logic would pass.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Duplicate `self.downsize` definition silently replaces the max_width/max_height version

The PR adds `def self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})` while the existing `def self.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` at line 145 is still present. In Ruby the later definition overwrites the earlier one, so the 5-argument form (from, to, max_width, max_height, opts) now raises ArgumentError. Any existing caller using that signature breaks. Only one of the two signatures should remain, or the callers should be updated and the old one removed.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify duplicate downsize definitions where the later dimensions-string signature overrides the earlier separate width/height signature, breaking existing callers.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client-side size check ignores the per-type site settings

`validateUploadedFile` previously used `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`. It now hardcodes 10MB for every upload type, so `max_attachment_size_kb` and `max_image_size_kb` are no longer respected by the client. Admin limits are bypassed in the UI, and attachments can be accepted up to 10MB even when the site caps them lower. The 413 handler at line 246 has the same hardcoding problem.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that hardcoding the upload limit to 10MB ignores per-type Discourse site settings, causing client/server limit divergence, and both flag the same problem in the 413 handler.

true_positives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Animated downsize passes a percentage to gifsicle --resize-fit

The controller calls `OptimizedImage.downsize(..., "80%", ...)`. For animated GIFs (when allow_animated_thumbnails is on), `downsize_instructions_animated` delegates to `resize_instructions_animated`, which emits `gifsicle --resize-fit 80%`. `--resize-fit` expects a WxH geometry, not a percentage, so the command will fail. `convert_with` then returns false silently, and the oversized GIF is uploaded anyway.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: animated GIF downsizing passes "80%" to gifsicle --resize-fit, which requires WxH geometry, causing downsizing to fail silently when animated thumbnails are enabled.

false_positives.candidate:
Downsize failures are ignored and oversized images are uploaded silently

`OptimizedImage.downsize` returns false on failure (convert_with swallows errors and returns false), but the return value is ignored. The loop runs at most 5 times and then falls through to `Upload.create_for` regardless of whether the file is still above max_image_size_kb. The user gets no error, and an image that exceeds the configured limit is stored. The loop should stop on a failed conversion and reject or report the upload if the file is still too large.

Remote URL download limit no longer follows the max_image_size_kb setting

The download size cap was changed from `SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` to a hardcoded `10.megabytes`. Admins who lower the setting will now have URL uploads accepted up to 10MB, and the setting is no longer enforced for this path. The image-downsizing change does not require this change to the cap, so the regression is unnecessary.

413 error message hardcodes 10 MB instead of the configured limit

The 413 branch now reports a fixed 10 MB limit instead of `Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb`. The displayed limit can be wrong for any site that has configured a different value, so the user is told the wrong maximum.

Commit/PR description is a placeholder

The PR description is just "Test 1" and does not explain the new behavior, the setting interaction, or the hardcoded 10MB change. A maintainer cannot review the intent or the regression risks from it.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
unsubscribe crashes when user has no TopicUser row

`tu = TopicUser.find_by(...)` may return nil (user never interacted with the topic, or is anonymous so current_user is nil). `tu.notification_level` then raises NoMethodError, producing a 500. Also `current_user.id` raises when not logged in, since unsubscribe is in the ensure_logged_in list only for the normal path; the lookup should handle a missing record, e.g. with TopicUser.change.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying issue: TopicUser.find_by may return nil when no record exists, and accessing tu.notification_level then raises an exception. The additional current_user concern does not negate the match.

true_positives.golden_comment: Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')
true_positives.matched_candidate:
misspelled property name stopNotificiationsText

The property is named `stopNotificiationsText` (extra 'i'), and the template references the same misspelling, so it works internally but the name is a typo that will confuse future maintainers and any other references.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same misspelled property, 'stopNotificiationsText', whose correct name is 'stopNotificationsText'. The differing description of the typo does not change the underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
unsubscribe toggles state in a non-idempotent way and ignores the intended action

The action flips the notification level: if currently above regular it sets regular, otherwise sets muted. Clicking an email unsubscribe link twice (or a mail client prefetch/scanner following the GET link) will alternate between muted and regular, re-subscribing the user. An unsubscribe link should set muted deterministically.

unsubscribe bypasses guardian checks and uses raw params for lookup

TopicView.new is built with params[:topic_id] which may be a slug-less id, and the TopicUser update uses params[:topic_id] directly without ensuring the topic is visible to the current user. Notifications are then changed for a topic the user may not be able to see; guardian.ensure_can_see! should be applied.

unsubscribe GET is state-changing and exempt from check_xhr and CSRF-protected flow

The unsubscribe endpoint mutates state on GET (and skip_before_filter :check_xhr is added), so any third-party page can trigger a muted change through an image or link for logged-in users (CSRF-like). Mutations should require POST or a signed token.

unsubscribe_url is hardcoded to the topic path and ignores the post number and slug

unsubscribe_url builds "#{url}/unsubscribe" from url(), which uses the current slug. Routes also add "t/:topic_id/unsubscribe" but the mailer now emits the slug form with `url` which may be a stale slug; the value is not validated against the actual route in the email, and the user_notifications path passes this URL into an email whose unsubscribe_link i18n key is also used by digest emails that do not provide unsubscribe_url, potentially rendering a broken %{unsubscribe_url} placeholder.

unsubscribe_link now references %{unsubscribe_url} for all emails

The shared unsubscribe_link string now contains %{unsubscribe_url}. Emails that add the unsubscribe link without passing unsubscribe_url (e.g. digest, admin or other MessageBuilder users with add_unsubscribe_link) will hit I18n interpolation errors or emit the literal placeholder text.

html template still uses %{unsubscribe_link} placeholder instead of the new per-topic link text

The template keeps only the generic %{unsubscribe_link} placeholder; the per-topic link text was added to the text/locale only, so the HTML email never shows the topic-specific unsubscribe option. Also `%{respond_instructions}` is now inside a div that previously had line breaks, which changes rendering but is minor.

unsubscribe strings contain HTML and unclear copy

stop_notifications contains raw <strong> markup inside a client string rendered with triple-stash in the template; the change_notification_state string lacks a trailing period, inconsistent with the other messages. Also the diff removes a blank line from an unrelated section.

unrelated formatting churn in topic_user.rb

Large whitespace and reformatting changes (scope, create_lookup, track_visit!) are unrelated to the unsubscribe feature and make review harder without functional benefit.

no tests for unsubscribe controller action or per-topic unsubscribe link

The only test change adds an unsubscribe_url option to a builder spec. No request spec covers the new TopicsController#unsubscribe action (mute/regular toggle, redirect, slug mismatch, anonymous access), and the message builder spec does not assert that the body contains the topic unsubscribe URL.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
true_positives.matched_candidate:
sed -i '' is macOS-only and the script runs unconditionally against the repo .env

`sed -i ''` fails on GNU/Linux, so the script breaks in Linux dev environments and CI. The script also rewrites ../.env in place without a backup, and the cleanup handler exits 0 even on the rate-limit failure path.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies that macOS-style `sed -i ''` fails on GNU/Linux, matching the golden comment's portability issue. The additional concerns do not change this match.

true_positives.golden_comment: Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Date formatting hard-coded to en-US and ignores user locale

The timestamp uses Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US") rather than the user's locale from useLocale, so the displayed date is inconsistent with the rest of the translated UI. Additionally new Date(cacheUpdatedAt) is called on a value that may arrive serialized as a string over tRPC, so the type annotation Date | null is not what is actually received at runtime.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies the same hardcoded en-US date formatting issue and failure to use the user's locale from useLocale. Its additional serialization concern does not negate this match.

false_positives.candidate:
deleteCache removes cache for any credential the user owns, not only Google Calendar, and ignores delegation credentials

The handler only checks that the credential belongs to the user, then deletes all calendarCache rows for that credentialId. The UI exposes this only for Google Calendar, but the endpoint itself accepts any credential id. Delegation-credential calendars are looked up by userId rather than credentialId in the cache repository, so deleting by credentialId will not clear the cache entries that are actually used for them, and the success response will mislead the user.

Cache status is queried on every connectedCalendars call, including for non-calendar and empty credential lists

getCacheStatusByCredentialIds is called unconditionally on every request to connectedCalendars, which is used across settings and onboarding pages. It runs a groupBy over CalendarCache for every call, even when there are no connected calendars. This adds a DB round trip to a hot read path just to populate a timestamp that is only displayed for Google Calendar.

groupBy on credentialId with empty array filter returns unexpected results and is not scoped to valid rows

When credentialIds is empty, Prisma's `in: []` yields no rows, which is fine, but the method also does not filter expired entries, so the 'last updated' timestamp shown reflects stale rows that were already expired or are being used for a different key. The status is per-credential max updatedAt across all keys, which does not represent whether the cache is currently valid.

updatedAt added with @updatedAt on a table that is written via upsert on userId-only paths

The new updatedAt column uses @default(now()) @updatedAt. Prisma's @updatedAt is set on every Prisma update, but the raw SQL migration uses DEFAULT NOW() with no matching trigger. Rows touched by raw SQL or by the legacy-userId update path will have inconsistent semantics, and the displayed 'last updated' value may not reflect when data was actually refreshed.

updateManyByCredentialId on every cache refresh bumps SelectedCalendar.updatedAt for all calendars of the credential

fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache now calls SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(credentialId, {}) after every cache write. This updates all selected calendar rows for the credential, including unrelated event-type scoped ones, on each refresh and webhook. It also has no effect on the UI as the PR notes, adding write load for no displayed value. The PR itself suggests it should be removed.

Dropdown hides cache deletion and disconnect for non-Google, and renders empty trigger when cacheUpdatedAt is a falsy-but-valid value

hasCache is `isGoogleCalendar && cacheUpdatedAt`, which returns the Date object or null. The conditional rendering is then mixed with the early return on `!canDisconnect && !hasCache`, so for a delegated Google credential with no cache the component returns null, but for a delegated Google credential with cache it still shows the trigger yet hides 'Remove app' correctly. Behavior is correct but fragile; more importantly the early return happens after hooks, which is fine, so the real issue is the 'Remove app' menu item is hidden when delegation is set while the cache-delete item shows without any confirmation context for delegated calendars.

deleteCache mutation onSuccess does not invalidate connectedCalendars, so cache status does not refresh

The deleteCache mutation's success handler only shows a toast and calls onSuccess. It does not invalidate trpc.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars, so the cacheUpdatedAt shown in the dropdown stays stale until a manual refresh, contrary to the PR's expectation that the UI updates.

deleteCache uses a raw z.number() input instead of a shared schema and does not check the credential type

The new procedure defines its input inline rather than in a schema file like the other calendar procedures. It accepts any credential id and no integration type, so the server contract allows deleting cache for non-calendar credentials.

Confirmation text says action cannot be undone but the cache is regenerated automatically

The 'confirm_delete_cache' string warns that the action cannot be undone, which overstates the impact since the cache is rebuilt on the next availability request. Also 'cache_last_updated' is passed a preformatted timestamp, so the translation key's placeholder name is coupled to the formatting done in the component.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.

Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working-hours end is computed from the slot start, so the end bound is never checked

`end` is computed from `slotStartTime` rather than the slot end, so `end === start`. The check `end > workingHour.endTime` therefore only tests the start time, and a slot starting inside working hours but running past the end is accepted. true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup code consumed non-atomically, allowing reuse via concurrent logins

The backup code is verified by reading the encrypted list, then writing back the list with the used entry nulled in a separate update. Two concurrent login requests with the same valid code can both read the unmodified list, both pass the indexOf check, and both succeed. A single-use code can therefore be replayed. The check and consumption need to be atomic (e.g., conditional update or transaction with compare-and-swap on the stored value).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race condition: backup code verification and consumption are non-atomic, so concurrent login requests can accept the same code more than once.

false_positives.candidate:
Used backup code is set to null but the code list is never pruned, and indexOf on null entries is fragile

Consumed entries are replaced with null in the array. Subsequent submissions of an empty or null-like input can match nulls in indexOf only if the input is null, and the request body backupCode is only checked for truthiness, so this is mostly safe; however the stored array keeps nulls forever and the JSON shape changes from string[] to (string|null)[], which the disable endpoint and any future reader must handle. Consider removing the entry instead.

Backup code verified without requiring 2FA enabled path to be sane; wrong input type can crash

req.body.backupCode.replaceAll is called on whatever the client sends. If backupCode is a non-string truthy value (number, object), replaceAll throws a TypeError causing a 500 instead of a 400. Also JSON.parse of decrypted data is unguarded.

Backup code used to disable 2FA is never consumed

The comment says the codes are deleted at the end, and the update sets backupCodes to null, so this does clear them on success. However the disable path with a backup code does not check that the code is still unused before the update, so concurrent requests can each disable 2FA with the same code; combined with the non-atomic pattern this is replay-prone. Same race as login.

Setup overwrites backup codes and stores them before 2FA is enabled, and returns them without a confirmation gate

Backup codes are written to the DB during setup while twoFactorEnabled stays false. Each setup call regenerates and replaces codes, which is intended, but the codes are shown to the user before they are verified and a backup code login path in login/next-auth checks only twoFactorEnabled, so this is acceptable only if the enable step is required. Additionally, symmetricEncrypt is called with process.env.CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY which is checked earlier, so ok; the real concern is that the plaintext codes are returned in the setup JSON response and cached by any intermediary.

Backup code blob URL is created on every setup and the previous one revoked by a stale closure

backupCodesUrl is read from component state inside handleSetup, so if state is stale the previous object URL may not be revoked, leaking blob URLs. The revoke condition relies on the previous render's value rather than a ref.

formatBackupCode is used before its declaration in handleSetup's closure order and the backup codes state is untyped

useState([]) gives an implicitly any[] state type, and formatBackupCode is a const declared after handleSetup; it works at call time but the untyped state hides shape errors. backupCodes should be typed as string[].

Closing the dialog after a backup code display does not reset the flow when the modal is dismissed via overlay

The Close button resets state, but dismissing the Dialog via onOpenChange (escape or overlay) skips resetState, so the backup codes step and the codes remain in state and the user can reopen into the DisplayBackupCodes step with stale codes.

Backup code login errors are mapped but the backup code field is never cleared, and password is still required

On an IncorrectBackupCode error, the form stays on the backup step with the old value; the errorMessages fallback and new branches are inconsistent with the errorMessages map used elsewhere. Also the 'Lost access' button clears only totpCode, not the password-related state, so the form submits with stale values.

resetForm called after success clears password field values but leaves the modal state stale on error paths

On failure paths the entered backup code or TOTP code is not cleared, so after an incorrect code the user must manually clear inputs; combined with the shared form, toggling Lost access does not clear errorMessage consistently.

Backup code login path bypasses the password check requirement ordering and TOTP fallback

When a backup code is supplied and the user has 2FA enabled, the TOTP branch is skipped entirely, but the earlier password check only runs when no totpCode is present. A request with totpCode and backupCode both present but no password skips password verification for CAL users whose password is set, since the password check is gated on !credentials.totpCode. The backup code path then succeeds without any password, which is an authentication bypass for users who know only a backup code and an email.

Migration adds column without considering existing 2FA users

Existing users who already have 2FA enabled get backupCodes null, so the backup code path returns MissingBackupCodes and they have no recovery path other than TOTP. This should be documented or the UI should prompt regeneration.

Backup code instruction text is inaccurate for the setup screen

backup_code_instructions says codes can be used to grant access without the authenticator, but it is also used as the description of the setup backup codes step, where the user is not told to save them now or that they are shown only once.

No test covers backup code login or the incorrect backup code path

The PR's stated test plan is to log in with backup codes, but no e2e test exercises that flow; the only new tests cover the setup download/copy and close buttons. The checklist also states no tests prove the feature works.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The exported function TwoFactor handles backup codes and is in BackupCode.tsx. Inconsistent naming.
Error message mentions 'backup code login' but this is a disable endpoint, not login

Backup code validation is case-sensitive due to the use of indexOf(). This causes validation to fail if a user enters uppercase hex characters, as backup codes should be case-insensitive for a better user experience.

Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.

The additionalNotes text was changed from 'organiser' to 'organizer' in createEvent. This is an unrelated text change that alters emitted notes content for existing users and is not part of the stated fix.

Lark createEvent ignores the credential and uses first destination calendar

Lark's createEvent takes the first destination calendar regardless of which credential is creating the event, so with multiple destination calendars across credentials, each Lark call uses the same calendar id and events are not created on the calendar each host expects.

This change, combined with requestedSlug still being set when IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED is true, results in both properties being set when billing is enabled, and neither when disabled

`await appStore[...]` now performs a dynamic import. If the key is unknown, `appStore[key]` is undefined and awaiting it yields undefined (handled), but if the module fails to load (missing module, build error) the rejection propagates out of getCalendar and every caller, which previously returned null gracefully. This changes failure behavior for calendar lookup.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
forEach with async callback discards promises; deletion errors and completion are not awaited

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => ...)` does not await the async callbacks. The surrounding try/catch can no longer catch errors from getCalendar or deleteEvent (they become unhandled rejections), and the function returns true before calendar/video cancellations finish, so the reschedule can complete while the old events still exist.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same async-forEach bug: callback promises are not awaited, errors escape surrounding try/catch blocks, and cleanup may remain incomplete when the function returns. Its narrower focus on event cancellations still matches the golden issue.

false_positives.candidate:
appStore entries are now un-awaited Promises, so consumers that index without await get a Promise object

The appStore object was changed from namespace imports to `import(...)` promises. Every consumer that reads `appStore[key]` and then checks `"lib" in app` or `"CalendarService" in app.lib` without awaiting will now get a Promise, where `"lib" in promise` is false, so the app is silently treated as not implemented. Any call site not updated in this diff (e.g. other files using appStore, getApps-related code, or the `as keyof typeof appStore` lookups) will break silently at runtime rather than fail at compile time, since the types still look plausible.

getCalendarCredentials still calls getCalendar synchronously, now receiving a Promise

getCalendarCredentials maps credentials with `const calendar = getCalendar(credential);` without await. getCalendar is now async, so `calendar` is a Promise stored in the returned array. getConnectedCalendars later does `await item.calendar`, but any other consumer of this function (and the type of the result) now deals with Promises, and the function itself is still synchronous so the calendar is created outside the await chain. Its errors also become unhandled promise rejections.

forEach with async callback discards promises; cancellation errors become unhandled

Same issue as the vital variant: the async forEach callback is not awaited, so the try/catch no longer catches calendar/video delete failures and they surface as unhandled promise rejections, while the function proceeds to send emails and return true before deletions complete.

forEach with async callback in requestReschedule; deletions not awaited and errors unhandled

`bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async ...)` fires calendar and video deletions without awaiting them. Errors become unhandled rejections (possibly crashing or spamming logs), and the mutation proceeds to send the reschedule email and webhooks while the previous calendar events may still be being deleted.

forEach with async callback inside recurring cancellation; apiDeletes is read before pushes happen

`.forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(...); ... apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent) })` is not awaited. `await apiDeletes` / `Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` runs before these async pushes occur, so recurring-event calendar deletions are neither awaited nor guaranteed to complete before the booking is reported cancelled, and failures are unhandled.

getCachedResults filters out nulls only after mapping, relying on index alignment that may now be wrong

Calendars are resolved with Promise.all over calendarCredentials, preserving order, so index matching still works, but the comment about nulls is now misleading and the resolved calendars are not paired with credentials after any filtering. Low risk on its own, but combined with other un-awaited uses it is fragile.

`await apiDeletes` awaits an array, not the pending deletions

`await apiDeletes;` on an array does not wait for any of the contained promises. The payment-rejection path therefore no longer waits for calendar/video deletions before returning success, which is the pre-existing bug, but the async conversion of getCalendar makes the pushed promises even more likely to be missing from this array.

Payment app lookup returns null from a function whose result is not a payment response; wrong type on fallback

In the refund path, when the payment app is not implemented the handler does `return null` from within handler, which is not a valid cancel response and skips cancellation entirely after the booking has already been deemed to need refund handling. true_positives.golden_comment: Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.

time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op in this test, so the wait for the flusher is not real

The comment says it gives flusher threads time to process after the drift change, but the call returns immediately. The test then calls `step.join()` and asserts on `messages`, so it can race with the flusher thread and fail intermittently. The wait needs to use a real sleep or a deterministic synchronization point.

The suggested fixes (real sleep or deterministic sync) align.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() stops waiting on deadline but does not terminate the remaining processes

In `join`, when the deadline passes the loop breaks before reaching the remaining processes, so those processes are never terminated. They are daemons, but the explicit termination step is skipped for them, so shutdown can leave child processes running.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same bug in join(): breaking the loop when the deadline elapses skips explicit termination of remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown.

false_positives.candidate:
--flusher-processes defaults to 1, so the PR's one-process-per-shard behavior is not the default

The new `--flusher-processes` option defaults to 1, and the factory forwards that value as `max_processes`. `SpanFlusher` then runs `min(max_processes, len(shards))` processes, so with the default every shard in the consumer is flushed by a single process. The PR description says the flusher should spawn a process per redis shard, but that only happens when operators pass a higher value explicitly. Either the default should be unset/None (meaning one process per shard) or the description and help text should say the default is a single process.

Hung thread-based flushers are restarted without being stopped

In `_ensure_processes_alive`, `process.kill()` is only called for `multiprocessing.Process`. For the `threading.Thread` path (used in tests with `produce_to_pipe`), a hung thread is left running and a second thread for the same shards is started. Both then flush the same buffer. false_positives.candidate:

getTokenContextFromTokenId splits on the first ':' and throws IllegalArgumentException if the prefix is not exactly 6 chars. Any token id from a non-standard source (or a raw UUID with a colon, or legacy formats) causes an exception rather than falling back to UNKNOWN as done for ids without ':'. Callers (introspection, userinfo) that receive such ids will fail with 500 instead of degrading gracefully.

Token type derived from request-wide client attribute, not from the token being created

getShouldUseLightweightToken(session) reads session.getContext().getClient(), which is the requesting client, not necessarily the client the token is issued for (e.g. token exchange to another audience, or refresh flows), and the token mapper logic uses the same helper. The encoded token type may not match the actual token format produced, making the encoded context unreliable for the stated use (lightweight detection).

Unsynchronized lazy refresh of shared maps on every miss

getShortcutByGrantType and getGrantTypeByShortcut mutate the shared ConcurrentHashMaps during token issuance and token id parsing. The grantsByShortcuts/grantsToShortcuts maps are also written without any atomicity across the two maps, so concurrent readers can see them inconsistent. Also, an attacker-supplied unknown shortcut in a token id triggers a full stream scan of provider factories on every request (no negative caching), a cheap DoS amplification.

postInit throws on duplicate shortcuts but init/postInit use non-thread-safe HashMap for shortcut tables

The shortcut validation compares map sizes, which only detects duplicate shortcuts that collide with the same key; if two grants share a shortcut, one silently overwrites the other in grantsByShortcuts and the sizes still differ only by accident. The size check is an indirect and incomplete duplicate detection. Also OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.getShortcut() has no default, so third-party grant factories break at compile/startup.

Cast of getProviderFactory result may throw ClassCastException

sessionFactory.getProviderFactory(OAuth2GrantType.class, grantType) returns a ProviderFactory that is cast directly to OAuth2GrantTypeFactory without checking; a non-OAuth2GrantTypeFactory implementation would fail at token issuance.

Token ID encoding can throw during token issuance for unregistered grant types

initToken calls encoder.encodeTokenId, which throws IllegalStateException when the grant type has no registered shortcut (e.g. a grant set on clientSessionCtx that is not an OAuth2GrantType factory, or tokens created by other paths that never set GRANT_TYPE, where the default 'na' is used). Token creation now fails for flows that previously worked, rather than falling back to a plain id.

Blank line removed while adding grant type attribute

The edit removes a blank line and inserts setAttribute in its place, which is cosmetic, but the attribute is set after the note and before the client is set; fine. Minor: no functional issue, included only as the diff replaced a blank line.

Refresh grant type set after the original grant type was lost; overrides initial value for refreshed tokens

validateToken sets GRANT_TYPE to refresh_token on the client session context, but this is only applied on the refresh path. Other paths (e.g. the RefreshTokenGrantType itself, which does not call createTokenResponse) rely on this implicit setting, so the encoded grant in tokens depends on which code path ran, making the encoded grant type inconsistent.

Grant type taken from context.getGrantType() which is the raw form parameter

context.getGrantType() returns the raw grant_type form parameter, which may be an arbitrary attacker-controlled string. It is stored as the grant type and, if it does not match a registered shortcut, encodeTokenId throws, causing a 500 instead of a proper OAuth error. Validation should happen before use.

true_positives.golden_comment: After creating the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel, consider setting its id from the stored credential (e.g., myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()); otherwise getId() will be null and downstream removal by id (e.g., removeStoredCredentialById in the authenticator flow) may not work.

updateCredential assigns a generated id to recoveryCodesModel, but getCredentials rebuilds the model with RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues(...), which does not copy that id. The returned credential therefore has no id matching the stored one. The authenticator then calls removeStoredCredentialById with that id once all codes are used, so the removal targets a non-existent credential and the spent codes remain stored.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel rebuilt via createFromValues omits the stored credential id, so getId() is null and removeStoredCredentialById cannot delete the spent recovery codes.

false_positives.candidate:
Recovery codes are written to user storage in plaintext

createRecoveryCodesCredential serializes the raw generatedCodes list to JSON and passes it as the credential data to user.credentialManager().updateCredential(). The local-storage path instead stores a RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel built from the same codes, which is designed to hold hashed codes (RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.hashRawCode exists for this). External user storage providers therefore receive and persist usable plaintext recovery codes, which a storage backend or anyone with read access to it can use to bypass MFA. The user-storage branch should store hashed codes, matching the local representation, and verification should compare hashes.

Recovery codes in user storage are never consumed after use

isValid for RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE only checks membership in the stored list and never removes or marks the used code. In local storage each code is single-use, so a code entered once can be entered again here indefinitely. The test provider also has no test asserting that a used code is rejected, so this gap is not caught. The provider's contract should require consuming the code, or the code should be documented as a limitation.

Removal of exhausted codes does not work for user-storage credentials

getCredential now returns federated (user storage) credentials first, but the removal call at line 86 uses credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(), which only operates on local-storage credentials. When the exhausted codes come from user storage, nothing is removed. The exhausted credential stays in storage, and getCredential keeps finding it on later logins. The removal should go through a path that handles federated credentials, or the mismatch should be handled explicitly.

Recreate exit code silently changed from 4 to 3

RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE changes from 4 to 3, and the new FEATURE_DISABLED takes 4. The update-compatibility command is documented as a scriptable, CI/CD-facing interface whose exit code is the contract. Any pipeline that already branches on exit code 4 for 'recreate required' will now treat it as 'feature disabled' and take the wrong action. The PR gives no rationale for renumbering an existing code instead of appending a new one. The comment about picocli ExitCode does not justify the value 3 either.

printFeatureDisabled hardcodes the string 'rolling-updates'. The feature key is available as Profile.Feature.ROLLING_UPDATES.getKey(), so if the key is ever renamed the message will silently diverge from the actual flag. The same literal is also duplicated in the test assertion and in the docs.

Overwrites user-configured enabled features in the test deployment

createInitialDeployment calls setEnabledFeatures(List.of(ROLLING_UPDATES)) unconditionally on the FeatureSpec. If getTestKeycloakDeployment or a caller already set enabled features, they are replaced rather than merged, so the test base configuration can be silently dropped and the test no longer exercises what it was written to exercise.

The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

The whole listener body is now wrapped in Profile.isFeatureEnabled(ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ). Previously it ran unconditionally. Under V2 (where only ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 may be enabled), role, client and group removal no longer clean up permission state. This behavior change is unrelated to adding clients and is not explained in the PR.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same bug: the AdminPermissions cleanup listener is incorrectly gated by the V1 feature flag, so when only V2 is enabled, role/client/group removal skips permission cleanup and leaves orphaned permission data.

In hasPermission(ClientModel, scope), if no per-client resource exists, the code loads the Clients type resource via getResourceTypeResource(). That method returns null when the schema is unsupported or the resource is not found. The result is passed straight to getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource) without a null check, which can throw an NPE instead of returning false.

false_positives.candidate:

With ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 enabled, management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2, whose clients() now returns ClientPermissionsV2. Its setPermissionsEnabled unconditionally throws UnsupportedOperationException. Deleting any client in a realm under V2 can therefore fail or leave the realm in a half-deleted state.

In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.

This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission collects resource names as IDs via findByType on the Groups type

In the V2 override, the granted IDs are added using groupResource.getId() (the Resource UUID), but the caller expects group IDs (the V1 implementation used resource name suffix). Group resources in V2 are typically named after the group id via the 'all-groups' type resource, so the stored value is the Resource entity id, not the group id. Callers (UserPermissions/UsersResource count and search) pass these to session.setAttribute(UserModel.GROUPS) and getUsersCount, which expect group model ids; the result will silently match no groups, so non-admin users with group-based VIEW_MEMBERS will see no members.

This mismatch causes group-based VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions to fail to match groups in user filters and counts.

false_positives.candidate:
hasPermission looks up resources by groupId as a resource name, but group resources are named by group id differently and falls back to type resource incorrectly

resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId) is used to find the group's resource, yet the 'all-groups' fallback uses getResourceTypeResource(...) and then checks policyStore.findByResource(server, resource). If the type resource is null (schema not initialized for the realm), resource.getScopes() / evaluatePermission will throw NPE at line 152 because resource is dereferenced without a null check on the fallback path.

canViewMembers/canManageMembers in V2 skip the group-independent MANAGE/VIEW fallback semantics and ignore user-level path

canViewMembers(group) only checks VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS on the group or all-groups resource. The V1 contract and the Javadoc in GroupPermissionEvaluator say a caller with MANAGE on the group should also view members; V2 canManageMembership checks MANAGE but canViewMembers does not, so behavior is inconsistent with the documented interface.

canViewByGroup now calls groups().canViewMembers, changing V1 semantics and recursion through hierarchy

canViewByGroup previously used getGroupsWithViewPermission(group) which returned true for users with view-users roles and checked VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS. It now delegates to canViewMembers, which itself returns true when root.users().canView(), causing redundant evaluation per group for every user in the stream filter, a performance regression on large user searches (each user triggers permission evaluation across its whole group hierarchy).

canManage/canView/canMapRoles pass group-check results but canMapRoles in V2 now ignores MAP_ROLES semantics for group members

canMapRoles in V2 now grants access when the user has MANAGE on the user or manage-members on a group, and the MAP_ROLES scope check is combined with MANAGE in a single OR. This broadens who can map roles compared to the previous MAP_ROLES-only check, a security-relevant permission widening that is not covered by any test in the PR.

Inconsistent use of group.getId() vs resource names for group lookup in canView/canManage

hasPermission(group.getId(), ...) calls resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId). Group resources in this PR are created by the schema with the group id as name (see AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup/getOrCreateResource), but GroupPermissions (V1) uses a 'group.resource.' prefix; any V2 group resource not yet created will fall through to the all-groups check and may grant access via the type-level permission without a per-group resource, which is intended but untested for the view path.

No test covers view of group members through GroupResource.getMembers or getSubGroups filtering

The new group-resource tests cover update/create/view listing, but never verify that a user with VIEW_MEMBERS can list members via /groups/{id}/members or that subgroup filtering in GroupResource.getSubGroups honours per-group view permissions after the canView(g) change. The regression risk from the removed canViewGlobal shortcut is untested.

getOrCreateResource switch without a default for null resourceType handled inconsistently

The switch on resourceType will throw NullPointerException if resourceType is null (switch on a null String), instead of the explicit IllegalStateException used for unknown types. Callers passing a null type from a malformed request will get a 500 instead of a validation error.

This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.

false_positives.candidate:
concatenatedRSToASN1DER builds r and s with a forced leading zero byte, producing non-minimal and wrong integers

The method copies each half of the signature into an array of length len+1 with a leading 0 byte, then calls new BigInteger(r). Shared queue pool is shut down when a rebalance closes the old strategy

`create_thread_queue_parallel_worker` hands the same `self.queue_pool` to every strategy it creates, and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()`/`terminate()` (queue_consumer.py ~lines 335-342) call `queue_pool.shutdown()`. On a Kafka rebalance, arroyo calls `create_with_partitions` again and closes the previous strategy. The old strategy's close shuts down the pool that the new strategy is using. Afterwards `FixedQueuePool.submit` calls `queue.put` on shut-down queues, which raises, and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` logs and silently drops the message while marking its offset complete. Result messages are lost after any rebalance. The pool lifetime needs to be owned by the factory, not by each strategy's close().

Offsets are committed from a background thread, not the processing thread

`_commit_loop` runs in its own thread and calls `self.commit_function(committable)`, which is the arroyo `commit` callable bound to the consumer. Arroyo/Kafka consumer commits are not designed to be called concurrently with the consumer's poll loop from another thread, and the strategy's `poll()`/`submit()` run on the processing thread. This can race with the consumer's own commit/poll or with rebalance handling and produce undefined commit behaviour. Commits should be triggered from the strategy's poll/submit path on the processing thread.

A single missing offset permanently stalls commits for the partition

In `get_committable_offsets`, the loop breaks at the first offset that is not in `all_offsets`. Kafka offsets are not guaranteed contiguous (log compaction, transaction control markers, aborted transactions). If an offset is never delivered to `submit`, `highest_committable` never advances past it, and every later offset is treated as blocked forever. Consumer lag then grows without bound and the committed position never moves, so on restart everything after the gap is reprocessed. The tracker should treat the gap as a non-outstanding position, e.g. by advancing over offsets that were never registered and were below the next delivered offset.

Queues are unbounded, so the advertised backpressure does not exist

The class docstring claims 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but every queue is created with `queue.Queue()` (no maxsize), and `submit` never blocks. The consumer will keep polling and buffering Kafka messages in memory whenever a slow worker falls behind, which can exhaust memory under a backlog. Either bound the queues and block or pause the consumer, or remove the claim from the docstring.

Shutdown discards queued work items without draining them

`FixedQueuePool.shutdown` sets `worker.shutdown = True` before shutting down the queues. The worker loop checks that flag before each `get`, so items still queued are abandoned rather than processed. Their offsets are never committed, so they will be reprocessed later. This is safe for at-least-once delivery, but it is not what the 'no item is lost' guarantee in the strategy docstring implies, and nothing logs how many items were dropped.

All factory tests create one strategy per factory and shut the factory down at the end. There is no test that calls `create_with_partitions` twice, closes the first strategy, and then submits to the second. Such a test would expose that closing one strategy shuts down the shared queue pool and drops messages.

The eviction policy is undocumented and the removed spans are never reported or metered. Also, `span_count` is derived from zunionstore/zcard results that were captured before the trim, and the max_segment_spans default of 1001 in buffer.py no longer matches the 1000 cap in Lua.

zunionstore with default aggregate SUM sums scores of duplicate members

Merging sets with `zunionstore ... 2 set_key span_key` uses the default SUM aggregation. Since the same span payload may exist in both sets (e.g. resent spans), its score is summed, corrupting the end-timestamp ordering that the eviction depends on. Using AGGREGATE MIN or MAX would be needed for correct scores.

Redirect-walk loop bound lowered from 10000 to 1000 without updating the documented limitation

The loop bound was reduced to 1000 and the comment about segment trees deeper than the limit was removed, so trees of depth 1000-10000 are now silently not joined, with no documentation of the new limit.

Negative offset is clamped to 0 for non-prev cursors, changing BasePaginator semantics

`start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` silently clamps negative offsets for next-page cursors, while the prior code passed them through. Combined with the Cursor change allowing negative offsets, a negative offset now returns the first page instead of being rejected or handled, a silent behavior change to all BasePaginator users.

OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates BasePaginator and has a missing key-order fix

The new class copies most of BasePaginator.get_result, and its build_queryset is inherited. Its `get_item_key` ignores post-processing semantics, and it is never covered by tests. Duplicated logic will drift and this class is dead code unless the audit log flag is kept.

Zset payload payload dedup and deleted span metadata break done_flush_segments and tests

Spans are now stored in a sorted set keyed by payload. The `_load_segment_data` loop uses `zscan` values as tuples but `payloads[key].extend(span for span, _ in zscan_values)` runs after the size check that already consumed them; flushed spans can therefore be double-counted in `sizes` across pages. Also `process_spans` now requires end_timestamp_precise, and any producer omitting it in `process_batch` causes a KeyError that crashes the batch.

Hard indexing of end_timestamp_precise can crash the whole batch

`val["end_timestamp_precise"]` raises KeyError for any span lacking the field, and `cast(SpanEvent, ...)` gives no runtime check. A single malformed message fails the entire processing batch instead of being skipped.

Comment claims negative offsets are supported but the Cursor type and callers do not handle them

The added comment says the cursor enables efficient reverse pagination for arbitrary positions, but nothing in build_cursor or the paginators validates or uses negative offsets for non-prev cursors. The comment misdescribes behavior and the change is a silent loosening of the cursor contract.

No tests added for the new negative-offset and optimized paginator behavior

The PR adds OptimizedCursorPaginator, negative-offset handling, the optimized_pagination endpoint branch, and the Lua eviction, yet only span-buffer test fixtures were updated to pass end_timestamp_precise. No test covers eviction above 1000 spans, the audit-log optimized path, or negative offsets.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

Cache key uses Python hash() of project list, which is randomized per process and can collide

The cache key embeds hash(tuple(sorted(project_ids))). Python's hash() for ints is deterministic, but the tuple hash is not guaranteed stable across processes and can collide; a collision would return another project set's eligibility for this org. The key also ignores that eligibility depends on the allowlist option, so a stale value can persist for 60s. Use the sorted project ids joined as a string instead.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that Python hash() makes the project-id cache key non-deterministic across processes and recommend a deterministic string representation of sorted project IDs.

Cached eligibility is returned without re-checking, and cache.get of False is treated as hit

The cache stores is_eligible and the cached path returns cached_result and transform check. This is consistent, but the cache is keyed only by org and project ids, not by the dataset/request, and the allowlist is also re-read fresh elsewhere, so the 'fresh' docstring contradicts the caching added in this PR. Behavior differs between cache hit and miss within the 60s window, producing inconsistent results for identical queries.

Allowlist membership compares ints against option values that may be strings

project_id in allowlist assumes the option stores integer ids. If the option is stored as strings (common for options edited via UI/JSON), no project matches and upsampling silently never applies; if types mismatch in the other direction, the check fails silently. The membership test should normalize types.

The transform replaces count() with an aliased function call regardless of whether the query's orderby, equations, or top-events column references 'count()'. Callers that look up the result by 'count()' key or pass the transformed columns into equations/orderby will break. The alias 'count' also may collide with a user-specified column of the same name.

upsampled_count ignores sample_weight existence and returns sum without guaranteeing column

The function assumes sample_weight exists for every event in allowlisted projects, but events without the context (for example, older SDKs or events stored before the change) have no sample_weight, so sum() undercounts them to zero or fails the query. The comment asserts a schema guarantee that the code does not enforce. The function also declares required_args=[] and default_result_type 'number' while it is used as an aggregate with the toInt64 wrapper, which truncates fractional sample weights.

Upsampling eligibility check runs on every _get_event_stats call, including per-bucket sub-queries

is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects is invoked at the top of _get_event_stats, which is called multiple times per request (split-query flow, transaction queries). Each call does a cache round trip and option lookup, undermining the claimed performance optimization. The comment 'cached result ensures consistent behavior' is misleading since the value is recomputed per call.

Top-events path transforms columns but the non-top-events path reuses the same final_columns variable incorrectly

final_columns is reassigned inside the RPC branch and the standard branch, but the upsampling transformation is applied to query_columns each time from the original input, so the behavior is correct only because the branches are exclusive. The duplicated transform blocks are fragile; a future edit that applies the transform earlier would double-transform. Hoisting one transformation is safer.

Error message text changed for existing clients

The response detail for topEvents <= 0 changed from 'If topEvents needs to be at least 1' to 'topEvents needs to be at least 1'. This is an unrelated behavior change in an upsampling PR that may break clients or tests matching the old string.

Docstrings and comments claim performance and consistency guarantees that are not true

Docstrings say the cache is 'safe because eventual consistency is acceptable' and that allowlist reads are 'fresh each time', which contradict each other and the caching added here. invalidate_upsampling_cache is defined but never called, so allowlist changes are not reflected for up to 60 seconds.

Factory silently swallows all exceptions when setting sample_rate

_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling wraps reads and conversions in bare 'except Exception: pass', hiding malformed test data and making tests pass or fail for the wrong reason. It also sets sample_rate on every stored event in test factories, which changes behavior of all tests that use store_event with error_sampling context.

setUp calls login_as(self.user) then reassigns self.user to a new user, so the logged-in user differs from self.user used in the event tags. The count assertions expect 10 for upsampled buckets (1 event at 0.1 rate) but nothing in the store path shows sample_weight is written, so these expectations are unverified and likely fail or pass for the wrong reason.

The transaction event is stored with a fixed trace id and no wait_for_event_count, so the snuba query can race and the assertions on data[0] and data[1] are flaky. The test also does not check the transaction path actually bypassed upsampling.

The PR adds a submodule pointer file 'sentry-repo' pointing at the base commit, and the description is 'Test 3'. These are unrelated artifacts that should not be merged into the repository.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache miss is re-checked only by the fast path, so concurrent callers all rebuild the manifest

The read lock is released at line 43 and the write lock is taken at line 48 without re-checking `entryPointAssetsCache`. When the cache is empty or in dev mode, every goroutine that misses the cache at the same moment proceeds to call readWebAssetsFromFile (or the CDN path) and rebuilds the manifest, one after another. The usual fix is to re-read the cache after acquiring the write lock and return early if it is already populated. This only matters at startup or in dev mode, so the impact is limited to redundant file reads and parsing.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same incomplete double-checked locking bug: after releasing the read lock and acquiring the write lock, the cache is not re-checked, so concurrent callers can all rebuild the manifest. The candidate also states the correct fix.

false_positives.candidate:
Write lock is held across file and network I/O, blocking all readers

The exclusive lock taken at line 48 is held for the whole rebuild, including the HTTP request in readWebAssetsFromCDN and the file read. Every concurrent GetWebAssets call, including ones that would otherwise hit the cached fast path, blocks on RLock until the rebuild finishes. A slow or hung CDN request, bounded only by the context, can stall all page renders. Consider doing the load outside the lock and only publishing the result under the lock.
